what-screening-is.title: What screening is, and what it is not
what-screening-is.inShort: Screening looks for cancer, or the stage before cancer, in people with no symptoms. In Finland it is free and voluntary, and you are invited by letter.

p: Screening can reveal a precancerous condition that can be treated before it becomes cancer. It can also find cancer early, when treatment is usually lighter and the outlook is better.
The tests are free of charge and voluntary. Wellbeing services counties organise them.
plain: Screening finds changes early. The tests are free. You choose whether to take part.

p: The national programme covers breast, cervical and colorectal cancer.
Systematic screening for prostate, lung and skin cancer does not currently meet the criteria for screening. Counties may still organise extra screening of their own.
plain: Finland screens for breast, cervical and bowel cancer. There is no national screening for prostate, lung or skin cancer.

stats.label: lower cervical cancer incidence, with screening
breast cancer deaths prevented in Finland each year
lower bowel cancer deaths, by current estimates

p: Taking part is voluntary. Counties must give residents enough information about the aims, organisation and effectiveness of screening, and about its possible risks.
Screening has downsides too. For example, some people are called for extra tests that turn out not to be needed. The breast screening article shows both sides.
plain: It is your choice. Screening has benefits and downsides. We show both.

breast-screening.title: Breast screening: what to expect
breast-screening.inShort: If you are 50 to 69, you get a letter about every 2 years inviting you for a mammogram. It is free. You choose whether to go.

p: Every woman aged 50 to 69 is invited by personal letter, about every 2 years. The letter gives a time and a place. You can change the time if it does not suit you.
If you do not want to take part, tell the screening unit. The letter explains how.
plain: Women aged 50 to 69 get a letter about every 2 years. You can change the time. You can also say no.

p: A mammogram is an X-ray of your breasts. Each breast is pressed between two plates, one at a time. You usually get the result by letter within a few weeks.
If the images show a change, you are invited for more tests. Most people who are called back do not have cancer.
plain: A mammogram is an X-ray. You get the result by letter in a few weeks. If the X-ray shows a change, you are called back. Most people called back do not have cancer.

stats.label: of those who take part are called back for more tests
of those called back have breast cancer

sections.lead: Screening helps some people and is not free of harm. You should see both before you decide.

cols.label: Benefit
cols.text: In Finland, deaths from breast cancer were 22% lower among women invited to screening between 1992 and 2003. Among women who actually went, they were 28% lower. A later study found the same.

cols.label: Downside
cols.text: About 1 in 5 women who go regularly are called for extra tests at least once that were not needed. Screening can also find small tumours that would never have caused symptoms. Studies suggest these are at most 1 in 10 of the tumours found.

p: Do not wait for your next screening. Contact your health centre, occupational health clinic or a private clinic.
plain: Do not wait for the next screening. Contact your health centre.

link.label: See the changes to look for

cervical-screening.title: Cervical screening and the HPV test
cervical-screening.inShort: Women aged 30 to 65 are invited about every 5 years. A nurse takes a sample, and a laboratory tests it for cell changes or for HPV.

p: Women aged 30 to 65 are invited every 5 years. In some counties, women aged 25 are invited too. The invitation arrives at your home, and you can change the appointment time.
plain: Women aged 30 to 65 get a letter every 5 years. You can change the time.

p: A nurse takes a sample from the cervix. It may pinch a little, and there may be some spotting afterwards.
Before the appointment you fill in a short form. It asks when your last period started, what contraception or hormone therapy you use, and when you last had a Pap test.
The sample is tested for cell changes (the Pap test) or for the human papillomavirus, HPV.
plain: A nurse takes a sample. It may pinch a little. A laboratory tests it.

p: A normal result means your next invitation comes after 5 years.
If the result is unclear, shows mild cell changes, or the HPV test is positive, you get another invitation after 1 to 2 years.
If stronger changes are found, you are invited for a colposcopy. Even then, the reason is almost always mild changes that are not cancer or a cancer precursor.
plain: Normal: next letter in 5 years. Unclear or mild changes: another test in 1 to 2 years. Stronger changes: a closer look called a colposcopy. This is almost always not cancer.

stats.label: lower cervical cancer incidence in Finland, with screening

p: Most cervical cancers are found in women who have not taken part in screening.
plain: Most cervical cancers are found in women who did not take part.

p: HPV causes cervical cancer and some other cancers. The vaccine can prevent infection with the HPV types that most often cause cancer. It protects best when given before sexual activity begins.
The Cancer Society page this is based on dates from 2017. Check THL for current vaccination programme rules.
plain: The HPV vaccine prevents infection with the virus types that most often cause cancer. It works best before sexual activity begins.

p: In 2026, people who are invited to screening in Central Finland, Kanta-Häme, Ostrobothnia, Pirkanmaa or Päijät-Häme can choose to take the sample at home, as part of a study. The kit is free.
You cannot order a kit without a screening invitation. If the HPV test is positive, you are referred for a sample at a clinic.
plain: In 5 counties you can take the sample at home, as part of a study. You need an invitation first.

link.label: Check if this applies to you

bowel-home-test.title: The bowel test you take at home
bowel-home-test.inShort: Every 2 years you get a letter with a test kit. You take a sample at home, post it, and get the result in about a month.

p: In 2026, people turning 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 70 and 72 are invited. You get a personal letter every 2 years.
Screening is being widened. By 2031 everyone aged 56 to 74 will be invited. It runs county by county.
plain: In 2026 people turning 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 70 or 72 are invited. By 2031 it will be everyone aged 56 to 74.

steps: The kit and instructions arrive with your invitation.
Fill in the preliminary information form that comes with the invitation.
Read the instructions and watch the sampling video.
Take the sample at home and put it in the return envelope.
Post the envelope within 24 hours. Postage is prepaid.
The laboratory looks for blood you cannot see.

p: You get the result within about a month of posting your sample, usually as an electronic message. Since 9 March 2026 it is also visible in MyKanta.
A normal result means no blood was found. Your next invitation comes in 2 years.
A positive result means blood was found. This is not necessarily cancer, but the cause must be found. You contact the screening nurse, and the next step is usually a colonoscopy.
plain: You get the result in about a month. Normal: no blood found. Positive: blood found. That is not always cancer, but you need a check.

p: Bowel cancer is the third most common cancer in Finland. More than 3,500 people are diagnosed each year, and about 1,300 die from it.

Early on, it often causes no symptoms or only vague ones. Screening can also find changes that can be removed before they become cancer. Current knowledge suggests it can prevent about one in six bowel cancer deaths.
plain: Bowel cancer is common in Finland. Early on it often has no symptoms. Screening can prevent about one in six deaths.

know-your-moles.title: Know your moles
know-your-moles.inShort: Learn what your moles normally look like. See a doctor if one changes or a new, different one appears.

p: Finnish adults have about 50 harmless moles on average. Watch moles that grow fast, change in appearance, become ulcerated or bleed. Also get a mole checked if it is reddening or shrinking.
Melanoma does not look like a normal mole. Its size, shape, colour and edges differ.
plain: Watch for a mole that grows fast, changes, bleeds, reddens or shrinks. See a doctor.

p: Check your skin regularly. Use a mirror for areas you cannot see. If a mole has changed, or you find a new one that looks somewhat different, see your doctor.
plain: Look at your skin. Use a mirror for your back. See a doctor about changes.

list: More than 100 moles
Sunburn, especially in childhood but also later
Skin that burns easily, freckles, ginger or fine blond hair
A family history of melanoma
Having had melanoma before
Atypical moles
p: Checking matters most if you have a sensitive skin type or other signs of higher melanoma risk.
plain: If you burn easily, have many moles or a family history, check more carefully.

stats.label: of skin cancers are due to solar UV radiation

p: Your behaviour in the sun can lower your risk significantly. Melanoma that can be removed by surgery has a good outlook.
plain: Protect your skin from the sun. Melanoma found early has a good outlook.

testicular-awareness.title: Testicular cancer: know your body
testicular-awareness.inShort: Testicular cancer is rare, and treatment results are very good. Know what is normal for you, and see a doctor about any change.

p: Testicular cancer is the most common cancer in men under 35, but it is rare. It is very rare over 45. Treatment results are extremely good, and cancer found early can be cured.
plain: It is rare. It is most common under 35. Found early, it can be cured.

steps: Examine both testicles, one after the other, with each hand.
Hold a testicle between your thumb and other fingers and rotate it.
Feel for lumps or changes on the surface of each testicle.
p: A normal testicle has an even surface and moves freely. You can clearly feel the epididymis behind it.

list: A lump in the testicle
One testicle getting bigger
A change in how firm a testicle feels
Pain
p: A tumour is usually a hard or rubbery lump inside the testicle. If you suspect something, see your doctor.
plain: A lump, a change in size or firmness, or pain. See your doctor.

breast-about.title: Breast cancer: the basics
breast-about.inShort: Breast cancer is cancer that starts in the breast. It is the most common cancer among women in Finland, and also in the UK.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Breast cancer is cancer that starts in the breast. It is the most common cancer among women in Finland, and also in the UK.
Anyone can get breast cancer, but it is much more common in older women.
In Finland, more than 60% of cases are found in women over 60. Only a few women under 25 get it each year.
Men can get breast cancer too. It is rare: about 30 cases a year in Finland.

list: Finland: about 5 200 women are diagnosed with breast cancer each year, says the Cancer Society page. Its short summary line says about 5 000.
Finland: in 2018–2022, about 5 000 breast cancers were found each year, per Finnish Cancer Registry figures quoted by the Cancer Society.
Finland: about 1 in 7 women gets breast cancer at some point in life.
Finland: more than 60% of breast cancers are found in women over 60. Just over 20% are found at ages 50–59, and just over 10% at ages 25–49.
Finland: breast cancer in men is rare, with about 30 cases a year.
Finland: about 40% of breast cancers are found by screening mammograms in women who have no symptoms.
Finland: lifestyle is estimated to cause about 30% of breast cancers. Being overweight and drinking alcohol together cause about 16%.
Older age. In Finland, the risk rises as women get older.
Hormones over a lifetime. Starting periods early or reaching menopause late raises the risk a little (NHS: before age 12, or after age 55).
Having no children, or having a first baby after age 30. Not breastfeeding also raises the risk.
Being overweight, especially after menopause, and drinking alcohol. These are the biggest risks you can change. In Finland, together they are estimated to cause about 16% of breast cancers.
Smoking. It gives a small rise in risk.
Some menopause hormone therapy (HRT) and the contraceptive pill raise the risk slightly. In Finland, HRT is estimated to cause about 2% of breast cancers.
Family history and inherited gene changes, such as BRCA1 and BRCA2. In Finland, about 10% of breast cancers are inherited.
Radiation treatment to the chest area at a young age.
Dense breast tissue, some non-cancer breast conditions, or having had breast cancer before.
Breast cancer cannot always be prevented, but some habits lower the chance.
Keep a healthy weight. The Finnish Cancer Society names overweight as one of the biggest risks you can change.
Drink less alcohol. The European Code says it is best to avoid alcoholic drinks.
Be active and eat a healthy diet. The Finnish Cancer Society says both seem to protect against breast cancer.
Do not smoke. The European Code advises against all tobacco and vaping.
Breastfeeding: the Finnish Cancer Society lists not breastfeeding as a risk factor. The European Code advises breastfeeding for as long as you can.
If you think about hormone therapy for menopause, talk it through with your doctor. The European Code says to use it for as short a time as possible.
Go to breast screening when you are invited. It can find cancers that are too small to see or feel.
If breast or ovarian cancer runs in your family, ask a doctor about genetic testing (NHS advice for the UK).

p: See a doctor soon if you find a lump or any change in your breast that is not normal for you. Most lumps are not cancer, but every lump should be checked.
The doctor examines your breasts. You usually have a breast X-ray (mammogram) and often an ultrasound scan. In special cases, an MRI scan is used.
To be sure, the doctor takes a small tissue sample (a biopsy), usually with a needle. A specialist checks it under a microscope. Only a biopsy can show for sure whether it is cancer.
The sample also shows what type of breast cancer it is. This helps the team choose the best treatment.
If cancer is found, more tests such as scans and blood tests show how far it has spread.
Treatment depends on how big the cancer is, what type it is and whether it has spread. Surgery is usually the main treatment. The surgeon removes either just the cancer area or the whole breast.
In Finland, surgery that keeps the breast is the first choice. It is almost always followed by radiotherapy. After a whole breast is removed, a new breast can often be built.
Other common treatments are chemotherapy, hormone therapy and targeted medicines. In Finland, hormone therapy usually lasts about five years, and sometimes up to ten.

cervical-about.title: Cervical cancer: the basics
cervical-about.inShort: Cervical cancer starts in the cervix, the neck of the womb where it joins the vagina. Almost all cases are caused by a long-lasting infection with certain types of HPV.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Cervical cancer starts in the cervix, the neck of the womb where it joins the vagina. Almost all cases are caused by a long-lasting infection with certain types of HPV.
People of any age who have a cervix can get cervical cancer. In Finland it is most common at ages 30–44 and very rare under 25.
You cannot get it if your womb and cervix were removed in a total hysterectomy.
A weak immune system raises the risk. WHO says women living with HIV are 6 times more likely to get cervical cancer than women without HIV.

list: Finland: about 170 cervical cancers are found each year.
Finland: since the national screening programme began in the 1960s, new cases have dropped to about one fifth of what they were.
Finland: the risk is highest in women aged 30–44. A bit more than one third of all cases are found at these ages. It is very rare under age 25.
Finland: HPV is found in over 90% of cervical cancers.
Finland: five years after diagnosis, 73% of women with cervical cancer are alive (no year given). If the cancer is found early and is confined to the womb, the outlook is 90%.
UK: cervical cancer is most common in women aged between 30 and 35, but it can happen at any age.
Finnish Cancer Society estimate (population not stated): about 80% of people get an HPV infection in their life. Most clear by themselves within a couple of years.
A long-lasting infection with a high-risk type of HPV. This is the main risk factor.
HPV spreads mostly through sexual contact. The NHS lists skin-to-skin genital contact, vaginal, anal or oral sex, and shared sex toys.
Smoking.
A weak immune system, for example from HIV.
Other sexually transmitted infections, especially chlamydia.
Starting sex at a young age and having several sexual partners are also listed as risk factors by the Finnish Cancer Society.
Having many children, or a first pregnancy at a young age. The NHS gives under 17 as the limit.
Using the contraceptive pill for a long time. The NHS says more than 5 years slightly raises the risk.
Get the HPV vaccine. It works best before sex starts. In Finland it is part of the national vaccination programme for girls and boys.
The vaccine in Finland's programme protects against HPV types 16 and 18. Other vaccines on the market cover more HPV types.
WHO advises HPV vaccination for girls aged 9–14. The European Code advises vaccinating girls and boys at the age recommended in your country.
Go to cervical screening. It finds pre-cancer cell changes so they can be treated before cancer forms. In Finland, screening has cut cervical cancer cases and deaths by up to 80%.
Still go to screening if you are vaccinated. WHO says pre-cancer rarely causes symptoms.
Do not smoke.
Condoms lower the chance of HPV, but do not fully protect. They do protect well against other infections such as chlamydia.

p: See a doctor if you notice unusual vaginal bleeding or discharge. Early cervical cancer often has no symptoms, so go to screening even when you feel well.
Serious cell changes are usually found first in a screening test (a Pap test or an HPV test). A doctor can also spot a problem during a gynaecological exam.

The next step is a colposcopy. The doctor looks closely at your cervix with a magnifying microscope that stays outside your body. Small tissue samples (biopsies) are taken. The biopsy confirms the diagnosis.
A colposcopy takes about 15–30 minutes (NHS). It is not meant to hurt, but it can feel uncomfortable.
If cancer is found, more tests show how far it has spread. These can include an exam by a gynaecologist, ultrasound or MRI scans, blood tests, and sometimes CT or PET scans.

Treatment depends on how far the cancer has spread and on your general health. Surgery is often the first choice, especially for cancers found early. If the cancer is found early and a woman hopes to have children, an operation that keeps the womb is sometimes possible.

If the cancer has spread to tissue around the cervix, doctors usually give radiotherapy together with chemotherapy (chemoradiotherapy). Targeted medicines or immunotherapy may be used for advanced cancer or cancer that has come back.
The Finnish Cancer Society says most cervical cancers can be treated with the aim of cure.

bowel-about.title: Bowel cancer: the basics
bowel-about.inShort: Bowel cancer, also called colorectal cancer, is cancer of the large bowel: the colon or the rectum. It almost always grows from a harmless growth in the bowel lining called an adenoma, which may look like a polyp.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Bowel cancer, also called colorectal cancer, is cancer of the large bowel: the colon or the rectum. It almost always grows from a harmless growth in the bowel lining called an adenoma, which may look like a polyp.
Bowel cancer affects both men and women. Risk rises with age.
In Finland, most people who get it are over 60, and the average age at diagnosis is 71. The NHS lists being over 50 as a risk factor.
People with a close relative who had bowel cancer, or with long-term bowel inflammation, have a higher risk.

list: Finland: more than 4 100 new bowel cancers are found each year, says the Cancer Society page (updated Sep 2026).
Finland: over 3 500 people get bowel cancer each year, and about 1 300 die of it, says the Fimlab screening page (Apr 2026).
Finland: bowel cancer is the third most common cancer, says Fimlab.
Finland: an older Cancer Society page (2022) also says third most common, with over 3 000 new cases a year.
Finland: most people who get bowel cancer are over 60. The average age at diagnosis is 71.
Finland: about 20–25% of people already have spread cancer when it is found.
Finland: five years after diagnosis, 70% of people with bowel cancer are alive. The outlook is clearly better when the cancer has not spread.
Older age.
A diet low in fibre and high in red meat and processed meat, such as sausage and ham.
Being overweight, drinking alcohol, smoking, and being inactive.
Long-term bowel inflammation, such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease.
Having polyps (small growths) in the bowel.
A close relative with bowel cancer, especially one diagnosed under age 45.
Inherited conditions such as Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).
Eat whole grains, vegetables, legumes and fruit as a big part of your meals. Eat less red meat and avoid processed meat. The NHS suggests five or more portions of fruit and veg each day.
Drink less alcohol. The European Code says it is best to avoid alcoholic drinks.
Be active in daily life and sit less.
Keep a healthy weight. Cut down on high-calorie, sugary, fatty and salty food and on ultra-processed food.
Do not smoke.
Take part in bowel screening when you are invited. It can find growths before they turn into cancer, and these can be removed.
If you have long-term bowel inflammation, follow your doctor's advice about regular bowel scope exams. The same applies if you carry a known family gene change such as Lynch syndrome.

p: See a doctor if you notice blood in your stool or a clear change in how your bowels work. Do not wait for a screening invitation. If your belly is very painful, you vomit and no stool passes, go to emergency care straight away.
The doctor may first feel the lower end of the rectum through the anus.

The main test is a bowel scope exam. A slim, bendable tube with a tiny camera is passed into the bowel so the doctor can see inside. It is called a colonoscopy when the whole large bowel is checked. It can feel unpleasant but does not usually cause strong pain. In the UK, sedation and pain relief are offered.
The doctor takes a small tissue sample (a biopsy) from any odd-looking area. A specialist checks it under a microscope. If a scope exam does not work, a CT scan of the bowel may be used.

If cancer is found, more tests show how far it has spread. Usually this is a whole-body CT scan. MRI or PET scans and blood tests are sometimes used. For rectal cancer, an MRI scan checks how far it has grown nearby.

Treatment depends on where in the bowel the cancer is, how far it has spread, and your general health. In most cases, doctors aim to remove the cancer with surgery. The surgeon takes out the tumour and part of the bowel, or sometimes all of it.

Chemotherapy may be given before surgery to shrink the cancer, or after surgery to lower the chance it comes back. Radiotherapy is mostly used for rectal cancer. In Finland it is usually given before surgery.

Some people need a stoma, an opening in the belly for stool. It can be temporary or permanent. If the cancer has spread to other organs, medicines can slow it down and ease symptoms. Chemotherapy is the main one, and targeted medicines or immunotherapy are used in chosen cases.

skin-about.title: Skin cancer: melanoma and other types
skin-about.inShort: Most skin cancer starts in the top layers of skin, where it can be seen. Basal cell and squamous cell cancers are common and usually treatable, and melanoma is rarer but more dangerous.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Most skin cancer starts in the top layers of skin, where it can be seen. Basal cell and squamous cell cancers are common and usually treatable, and melanoma is rarer but more dangerous.
Skin cancer is common. Basal cell cancer is the most common type, and squamous cell cancer is less common. Melanoma is rarer but the most dangerous.
UV light from the sun and from sunbeds is the main cause. What matters most is the total UV you get across your whole life. So the risk is highest in older people and in people who work outdoors.
Melanoma affects women and men almost equally in Finland. It is more common in older people, but younger people can get it too.
People with brown or black skin are less likely to get skin cancer, but it can still happen. In them, melanoma most often appears on the soles of the feet, palms of the hands or under a nail.

list: Finland: about 1,800 people are diagnosed with melanoma each year, and it is almost equally common in women and men.
Finland: about 90% of people with melanoma live more than 5 years after diagnosis.
Finland: about 9900 basal cell cancers are recorded each year. The true number is probably much higher, because not all are recorded.
Finland: just under 1900 squamous cell cancers are found each year.
Finland: the 5-year survival rate for squamous cell cancer is 94%.
Finland: on average 1 in 3 people treated for basal cell cancer gets a new one within 5 years.
Finland: 20 to 30% of melanomas start in an existing mole. The rest appear as a new spot on skin that was healthy before.
UV light from the sun and from sunbeds (the most important cause)
A lot of sun exposure over your lifetime, for example from outdoor work
Sunburn, especially repeated burns in childhood
Using sunbeds or a solarium
Pale skin that burns easily, red or fair hair, blue or green eyes, many freckles
A large number of moles, or unusual-looking moles (dysplastic naevi)
A very large mole that you were born with (over 20 cm wide)
Skin cancer in your family, or having had skin cancer before (including an earlier melanoma)
Having had an organ transplant (a higher melanoma risk)
Getting older
Long-lasting wounds or irritated scars, where squamous cell cancer can sometimes begin
Avoid too much sun, especially for children, and use sun protection.
Do not use sunbeds.
Stay out of the sun in the hottest part of the day (the NHS gives 11am to 3pm for the UK).
Cover your arms and legs. Wear a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses that block UV rays.
Use sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and at least 4-star UVA protection, and put it on again regularly.
Protect babies and children carefully. Their skin is much more sensitive than adult skin.
Check your skin now and then, and get changes looked at early.

p: See a doctor if a mole changes size, shape or colour, or is painful, itchy, inflamed, bleeding or crusty. Also go if a new or odd mark has not gone away after a few weeks, or a sore does not heal. Do not wait because a spot is painless, as not all skin cancers hurt. If you notice two or more warning signs, do not delay. In Finland, the 'VARO' check lists four warning signs: uneven colour, a width over 6 mm, an irregular edge, and uneven halves. Show any such mole to a doctor. Small dark dots appearing around a mole are always a sign of melanoma. To check hard-to-see areas, use a mirror or ask a friend or partner. Photos with a ruler next to the spot help you notice changes. The doctor may photograph the mole to send to a skin specialist.
A doctor looks at your skin, sometimes with a magnifying device, and asks about any changes you have noticed.

For melanoma, the mole is cut out with a small edge of skin and sent to a lab (an excision biopsy). Results usually take about 2 weeks. In Finland, if melanoma is found, a second operation usually removes more skin around the scar.

For basal cell cancer, the look of the spot often points to the diagnosis, but a tissue sample confirms it. Small spots are often cut out whole. For squamous cell cancer, a tissue sample is taken, and nearby lymph nodes are sampled if they feel enlarged.

If cancer is found, more tests show how deep it is and whether it has spread. These can include CT or MRI scans, lymph node tests and blood tests. Basal cell cancer rarely spreads, so these tests are seldom needed.
Surgery is the main treatment for melanoma. The surgeon removes the melanoma and a rim of healthy skin around it. A large area may need a skin graft.

Surgery is also the main treatment for basal and squamous cell cancers. In Finland, almost all basal cell cancers can be cured by surgery. Small, thin ones can sometimes be frozen, treated with a laser, a light-sensitive medicine (photodynamic therapy) or a cream. Radiotherapy is used in special cases.

For melanoma that has spread, medicines are the usual treatment: immunotherapy and targeted medicines. In Finland, about 40 to 50% of melanomas have a BRAF gene change that targeted medicines can treat. Radiotherapy is sometimes used, and chemotherapy is rarely used now.

Finland has no national skin cancer screening programme. Its national programmes cover only breast, cervical and colorectal cancer. In the UK, there is no national melanoma screening programme (Cancer Research UK). Research has not shown that the benefits outweigh the risks. The best way to find melanoma early is to know the signs and see a doctor if you notice any. People at higher risk can have skin checks by a specialist. Euromelanoma advises checking your skin for changes, using the ABCDE signs and the 'ugly duckling' sign.

prostate-about.title: Prostate cancer: the basics
prostate-about.inShort: Prostate cancer starts in the prostate, a small gland under the bladder. It is the most common cancer in men in Finland, and it often grows slowly.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Prostate cancer starts in the prostate, a small gland under the bladder. It is the most common cancer in men in Finland, and it often grows slowly.
The prostate is a small gland under the bladder, about the size of a walnut. It makes the fluid that mixes with sperm to form semen.
In Finland, prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men, with about 5000 new cases a year. It mainly affects older men, mostly over 70.
Anyone who has a prostate can get it, including some trans women and non-binary people who were born male.

NHS says it mostly affects men over 50. Men of Black African or African Caribbean background have a higher chance. Finnish experts say dark-skinned men have a higher risk of the aggressive form and are diagnosed at a younger age.

list: Finland: prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men, with about 5000 men diagnosed each year.
Finland: it is mainly a disease of men over 70. It becomes clearly more common after age 55 and is very rare under 40.
Finland: about 5 to 10% of prostate cancers are an inherited type.
Finland: 94% of men with prostate cancer are alive 5 years after diagnosis.
Finland: up to half of cancers found by PSA screening would never have harmed the man during his lifetime.
UK source: 1 in 6 men in the UK will get prostate cancer at some point. It is most common at ages 75 to 79.
UK source: studies show around 15 in 100 men with a normal PSA level have prostate cancer (the test misses it).
Age. This is the biggest single risk factor.
Having a father, brother or other close male relative with prostate cancer, especially if diagnosed before age 60
A close relative with breast, ovarian or pancreatic cancer, especially at a young age
An inherited gene change, most often in the BRCA2 gene, or Lynch syndrome
Black African or African Caribbean background (a higher chance of the aggressive type in Finnish information)
Being overweight or obese
A diet high in fat (Finnish information)
Smoking (it raises the chance of dying from prostate cancer)
Heavy exposure to pesticides (most people only meet small amounts)
There is no proven way to prevent prostate cancer. Cancer Research UK says it is not clearly linked to any preventable cause.
Keep to a healthy weight. Obesity may be linked to a higher risk of cancer that has spread.
Stay active. Finnish information says regular exercise clearly lowers the chance of dying from prostate cancer, though its effect on getting it is unclear.
Do not smoke.
If prostate, breast, ovarian or pancreatic cancer runs in your family, talk to a doctor about your risk, even without symptoms.

p: See a doctor if you have trouble peeing or any other symptom above. Also go if your symptoms change, get worse or do not feel normal. These symptoms are most often caused by a harmless enlarged prostate, but they still need checking. Men over 40 who know they carry a faulty BRCA2 gene should also see a doctor. You can ask about a PSA blood test even without symptoms, and the doctor will go through the pros and cons with you. In the UK, a doctor who suspects cancer, or sees a high PSA result, may arrange an urgent referral. This does not definitely mean you have cancer.

A doctor may feel the prostate through the back passage (rectal exam) and take a PSA blood test. PSA is a protein made by the prostate. A raised PSA can mean cancer, but also infection or an enlarged prostate.
A normal PSA does not rule out cancer, and no single PSA number proves it. In Finland, doctors also look at the share of 'free' PSA and at your age.
If something looks wrong, you have an MRI scan of the prostate to show suspicious areas.

A biopsy then takes small tissue samples with a needle. In Finland, samples are taken through the wall of the rectum with antibiotics to prevent infection. A pathologist checks them under a microscope and gives a Gleason score, which shows how aggressive the cancer is.
Bone scans, CT, MRI or PET scans may be used to check whether the cancer has spread.

Not every prostate cancer needs treatment. Slow-growing cancers can be watched with regular tests (active surveillance or watchful waiting). In Finland, low-risk cancer is usually watched this way to avoid over-treatment.

Cancer that has not spread can often be treated with surgery to remove the prostate, or with radiotherapy. In Finland, radiotherapy is now the most common choice. Both can cause side effects, such as leaking urine and erection problems.
Hormone therapy lowers testosterone, which feeds the cancer. It is used with radiotherapy for early cancer and to slow advanced cancer. Chemotherapy may be added if the cancer has spread.

Finland has no national prostate cancer screening programme. Its national programmes cover only breast, cervical and colorectal cancer. The Cancer Society of Finland says men without symptoms should not routinely have a PSA test. An exception is a good reason, such as a family history. It says the harms of PSA-only screening outweigh the benefits, including false alarms and treating cancers that would never cause harm. In December 2022, the Council of the EU asked member states to evaluate organised screening using PSA plus MRI follow-up. This invites countries to study it; it does not require screening. Finland is running a large trial called ProScreen (120,000 men) to test this. In the UK, screening all men is not recommended. Targeted screening is planned from 2027 in England. It is for men aged 45 to 61 with a BRCA2 gene change and a relevant family history.

testicular-about.title: Testicular cancer: the basics
testicular-about.inShort: Testicular cancer starts in a testicle, usually just one. It is rare, it mostly affects younger men, and it is usually found early and treated well.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Testicular cancer starts in a testicle, usually just one. It is rare, it mostly affects younger men, and it is usually found early and treated well.
Testicular cancer is rare, but it is the most common cancer in young men in Finland. In Finland it is most common at ages 25 to 39. In the UK it mostly affects men aged 15 to 49.
Anyone who has testicles can get it. It usually affects only one testicle, but it can affect both.
There are two main types, seminoma and non-seminoma. Both are treated well, and seminoma has a slightly better outlook.

list: Finland: only about 170 new testicular cancers are found each year, so it is a rare cancer.
Finland: it is the most common cancer in young men, and is most common at ages 25 to 39.
Finland: one main type (non-seminoma) is most common at ages 25 to 29, and the other (seminoma) at ages 30 to 34.
Finland: 95% of patients are alive 5 years after diagnosis.
Finland: cancer is usually found in only one testicle.
Finland: an undescended testicle raises the risk almost 4-fold, but the risk is still under 1%.
Finland: a brother of a patient has an 8-fold risk, and a father or son has a 4-fold risk.
Having an undescended testicle, now or in the past
A brother, father or son who has had testicular cancer
Having had testicular cancer before
Hypospadias, where the opening of the urethra is not at the tip of the penis
Having HIV or AIDS
White British background (a UK finding)
There is no proven way to prevent testicular cancer. Finnish experts say its causes are not known.
Get to know how your testicles normally look and feel, so changes stand out.
Look and feel now and then, for example during or after a warm bath or shower. Get any change checked early.
After treatment, healthy living and not smoking are important.

p: See a doctor if you notice any lump or swelling on a testicle. Also go if a testicle gets bigger, your scrotum feels heavy, firm or hard, or you have an ache or pain. Any change that is not normal for you is worth checking. This includes a lump or change in the soft tube at the back of a testicle. In Finland, every lump or swelling in a testicle is a reason to see a doctor. Most lumps are not cancer, and other causes exist, such as a fluid-filled cyst. Urgent: in young people, sudden pain in the scrotum can be a twisted testicle (torsion). It always needs immediate surgery. Try not to feel embarrassed. Doctors are used to these problems.
The doctor feels both testicles and checks the lymph nodes at the top of your legs. In Finland, the exam starts with the normal testicle for comparison.
A doctor may shine a bright light through the scrotum. Light passes through a fluid-filled cyst but not through a solid cancer.
An ultrasound scan of the testicles shows whether the lump is inside or outside the testicle. In Finland, no needle biopsy is needed.
Blood tests check markers that many testicular cancers release (AFP and hCG in Finland). Normal results do not rule cancer out.
The diagnosis is confirmed by surgery that removes the testicle and the tumour. Scans of the belly and chest (CT, sometimes MRI or PET) show if it has spread.

Surgery to remove the affected testicle (orchidectomy) is the first treatment for nearly all testicular cancers. For some people it is the only treatment. You can usually choose to have an artificial testicle placed.

After surgery, you may have careful follow-up, chemotherapy, or sometimes radiotherapy. Chemotherapy is usually needed if the cancer has spread. In Finland, the standard drug combinations are called BEP and EP.

Some treatment can affect fertility, so you are offered sperm banking beforehand. Removing one testicle does not usually affect fertility or sex life, because the healthy testicle keeps making testosterone and sperm.

There is no national screening programme for testicular cancer in the UK, because no reliable test finds it early. Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and colorectal cancer. Checking your own testicles is not the same as screening. The NHS suggests checking about once a month from puberty, ideally during or after a warm bath or shower. Cancer Research UK says there is no need for a set routine. It notes there is little evidence that regular self-checks in a set way help. Both agree it is useful to know what is normal for you and to get any change checked.

lung-about.title: Lung cancer: the basics
lung-about.inShort: Lung cancer starts in one or both lungs. It is one of the three most common cancers in Finland, and smoking is its biggest risk factor.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Lung cancer starts in one or both lungs. It is one of the three most common cancers in Finland, and smoking is its biggest risk factor.
Lung cancer mostly affects older people. In Finland it is most common after age 70. Only about 1 in 10 cases is found before age 60.
In Finland, men get it nearly twice as often as women when age is taken into account. The share of women is growing, and the Cancer Society links this to more women smoking.
Smokers are at highest risk, but people who never smoked can get it too.

list: Finland: lung cancer is the third most common cancer in both men and women, with about 3,000 new cases a year.
Finland, 2022: 1,740 men and 1,207 women were diagnosed with lung cancer.
Finland: about 9 in 10 lung cancers are caused by smoking. A smoker's risk is 15 to 30 times higher than for someone who never smoked.
Finland: about 4 in 10 lung cancers are found in women. Only about 1 in 10 are found in people under 60.
Finland: about 1 in 10 people with lung cancer never smoked.
Finland: the Cancer Society says 13% of men and 21% of women are alive five years after a lung cancer diagnosis.
Finland: the 2026 national lung cancer programme gives about 17% of men and about 26% of women alive after five years. Finnish results are worse than in other Nordic countries.
Smoking. The earlier you start and the more and longer you smoke, the higher the risk.
Breathing other people's smoke over a long time (passive smoking)
Work or home exposure to asbestos, silica, diesel exhaust, or arsenic, nickel and chromium compounds
Radon, a natural gas that can build up inside buildings
Breathing polluted air over many years
Lung diseases such as COPD, and past tuberculosis (Finnish source)
A close relative who has had lung cancer
Do not smoke, or stop if you do. After about ten years smoke-free, risk falls a lot but stays slightly higher than for people who never smoked.
Avoid other people's smoke. In Finland, passive smoking is said to raise risk 2 to 3 times.
If you smoke and also work with asbestos, quitting matters even more. The Cancer Society says asbestos can raise a smoker's risk up to 50 times.
If you live somewhere with high radon, stopping smoking is even more important.
Keep active with regular exercise.
Eat a healthy diet with five servings of fruit and vegetables each day.

p: See a doctor if you have a cough that lasts more than 3 weeks, or any other symptom on this list. Get urgent medical advice if you cough up blood. Get emergency help if you struggle to breathe, or have pain in your chest or upper back. Lung cancer often causes no symptoms early on, and these signs have other common causes. Still, getting checked is important, because finding it early may make it easier to treat.
The doctor asks about your symptoms and listens to your chest. You may have a blood test or a chest X-ray. In Finland the first step is usually a chest X-ray. It shows tumours bigger than about 1 cm.

The main tests are a CT scan and a bronchoscopy. In a bronchoscopy, a thin, bendy tube with a tiny camera goes down your throat into your lungs. The doctor can look inside and take small tissue samples (biopsies).
If the tumour is not near an airway, a needle may be used through the skin to take a sample (Finland).
Blood tests cannot diagnose lung cancer. In Finland they are used to check general health and how the liver and kidneys work.
After a diagnosis you may need more tests, such as MRI, PET scans, biopsies, blood tests and gene tests. These show the type, how far it has spread, and gene changes, which helps choose treatment.

Treatment depends on the type of lung cancer, its size, whether it has spread, gene changes, and your health. The main treatments are surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted medicines or immunotherapy. They are often combined.
Surgery is the main treatment aimed at cure for non-small-cell lung cancer. In Finland, fewer than a quarter of lung cancers can be operated on. Most have already spread when they are found.
If the cancer has spread and cannot be cured, treatment aims to slow it, ease symptoms and help people live longer. A palliative care team supports comfort and other needs.

Finland has no national lung cancer screening programme. Finland's national programmes are only for breast, cervical and colorectal cancer. The Finnish Cancer Registry says CT scans of smokers cut lung cancer deaths by one-fifth. It did not recommend screening, because of many unnecessary follow-up tests. Finland's national lung cancer programme (2026 to 2035) will now look at screening people at higher risk. In England, the NHS offers lung health checks in some areas. They are for people aged 55 to 74 who have ever smoked, and targeted screening is being rolled out. In the UK, the National Screening Committee recommends targeted screening for people at high risk.

stomach-about.title: Stomach cancer: the basics
stomach-about.inShort: Stomach cancer starts in the stomach, the organ that helps digest food. It has become much less common in Finland, but it can stay silent for a long time.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Stomach cancer starts in the stomach, the organ that helps digest food. It has become much less common in Finland, but it can stay silent for a long time.
Anyone can get stomach cancer, but it is more likely if you are over 50 or a man (NHS, UK).
A parent, brother or sister who had stomach cancer also raises your risk.
In Finland it was once the most common cancer. Now about 640 people a year are diagnosed.

list: Finland: about 640 new stomach cancers are found each year.
Finland: new stomach cancer cases have fallen to about one-tenth of the 1950s level, when it was the most common cancer in both men and women.
Finland: about 95 in 100 stomach cancers are adenocarcinomas, which start in the gland cells of the stomach lining.
Finland: when stomach cancer is diagnosed, only about 1 in 3 is still limited to the stomach.
Finland: about 1 in 3 people with stomach cancer are alive five years after diagnosis.
Worldwide: stomach cancer is the fifth most common cancer (as stated by the Cancer Society of Finland).
UK: the NHS describes stomach cancer as not very common.
Long-term infection of the stomach lining with the germ Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori)
Long-term stomach inflammation (gastritis), including the thinning type, and stomach polyps (small growths)
Pernicious anaemia, where the body cannot absorb vitamin B12 well
Long-term, severe acid reflux
A stomach ulcer, or a stomach that has had part of it removed in the past
Smoking
Eating a lot of salt and few fresh vegetables and fruit
A brother, sister or parent who had stomach cancer, and some inherited factors
Being over 50, and being male
Stop smoking, or try to quit.
Eat less salt.
Aim for five or more servings of mixed fruit and vegetables each day.
Cut down on alcohol.
If you carry extra weight, work towards a healthier weight.
Use protective clothing and masks if your job exposes you to harmful chemicals (the NHS names rubber and coal-mining work).

p: See a doctor if you have trouble swallowing, a lump in your tummy, or weight loss you cannot explain by diet or exercise. Also go if stomach symptoms get worse or do not improve after 3 weeks. In Finland the Cancer Society adds more signs. Go if upper-tummy trouble first starts at about 50 to 55 or older. Go too if you vomit again and again, vomit blood, pass black stool, or have new anaemia. Get urgent advice if you are being sick for more than 2 days. Early stomach cancer can feel like other stomach problems, so tell your doctor if your usual symptoms change.
The doctor may feel your tummy and ask for a blood, poo or pee sample.

The main test is a gastroscopy. A thin, bendy tube with a camera goes through your mouth into your stomach. It takes about 10 to 15 minutes. You can have throat-numbing spray or medicine to help you relax.
Small tissue samples (biopsies) are taken and checked in a lab. This is how cancer is confirmed. Blood tests alone cannot diagnose stomach cancer (Finland).
If cancer is found, scans (CT, ultrasound from inside using the scope, or PET) and sometimes keyhole surgery show how far it has spread.
Treatment depends on the size and place of the cancer, whether it has spread, and your health. It usually includes surgery and chemotherapy. Radiotherapy and targeted medicines are sometimes added.
Surgery removes part or all of the stomach, and sometimes parts of nearby organs. In Finland it is the first choice. It can cure the cancer if found before it spreads past the nearby lymph nodes.
Chemotherapy before or after surgery lowers the chance of the cancer coming back. After the whole stomach is removed, people eat small meals often and need vitamin B12 replacement for life (Finland).

Finland has no screening programme for stomach cancer. The Finnish Cancer Registry says screening is not considered necessary in countries with few stomach cancers, such as Finland. Finland's national screening programmes are only for breast, cervical and colorectal cancer.

thyroid-about.title: Thyroid cancer: the basics
thyroid-about.inShort: Thyroid cancer starts in the thyroid, a small gland low in the front of the neck that makes hormones. Most cases have a good outlook.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Thyroid cancer starts in the thyroid, a small gland low in the front of the neck that makes hormones. Most cases have a good outlook.
Thyroid cancer is rare overall, and it is more common in women. In Finland, about twice as many women as men are diagnosed.
In Finland, the most common types usually appear between ages 45 and 70. The most common type, papillary cancer, is often found in younger women.
In the UK, women are most often diagnosed in their early 40s and men in their 70s.

list: Finland: about 500 people get thyroid cancer each year.
Finland: thyroid cancer is about twice as common in women as in men.
Finland: 92% of people with thyroid cancer are alive five years after diagnosis.
Finland: about 80% of thyroid cancers are the papillary type, and about 10% are the follicular type.
Finland: about 1 in 10 people have a thyroid lump that can be felt. Most of these lumps are not cancer.
UK: fewer than 10 in 100 thyroid lumps are cancer.
UK: thyroid cancer in women peaks at ages 40 to 44. In men it peaks at ages 75 to 79.
Radiation to the neck area, such as radiotherapy years ago, especially in childhood
Being overweight or obese
Some non-cancerous thyroid conditions: goitre (swollen thyroid), Hashimoto's disease, or thyroid nodules (lumps)
A close family member who had thyroid cancer, and rare inherited gene changes
Having had certain other cancers, such as breast, oesophageal or testicular cancer, or non-Hodgkin lymphoma
In most cases, no cause is found
You cannot always prevent thyroid cancer, but healthy habits can lower the chance of it and other cancers.
If you carry extra weight, work towards a healthier weight.
Cut down on alcohol.

p: See a doctor if you find a lump in your neck, even if it does not hurt. Also go if your voice stays hoarse, swallowing stays difficult, or you have neck pain or a feeling of pressure. See a doctor again if a lump you had checked suddenly grows. Get urgent help if you have trouble breathing or are more short of breath than usual. Most lumps and these symptoms are not cancer, but a check is important because early cancer may be easier to treat.
The doctor may feel your neck and arrange a blood test.
In Finland, thyroid cancer is diagnosed with an ultrasound scan of the neck and a thin-needle sample from the lump. Taking the sample is almost painless.

Some thyroid cancers, the follicular type, can be confirmed only after surgery, when the whole lump is examined. In Finland, blood tests cannot show thyroid cancer. It does not usually change how the thyroid works.
If cancer is found, you may need CT, MRI or PET scans. You may also have a thin camera tube passed through the nose to check your vocal cords.
Surgery is the main treatment. Doctors remove all or part of the thyroid, and sometimes lymph glands in the neck.

After the whole thyroid is removed, you take thyroid hormone tablets for life. Radioactive iodine (a tablet or drink) after surgery can destroy any thyroid or cancer cells left behind. It does not work for the medullary type.
Radiotherapy, targeted medicines and chemotherapy are used less often. They are mostly for cancer that cannot be removed, has come back, or has spread.

Finland has no national screening programme for thyroid cancer. Finland's national screening programmes are only for cervical, breast and colorectal cancer, and the Finnish Cancer Registry's screening page does not mention thyroid. If you find a lump in your neck, see a doctor.

mouththroat-about.title: Mouth and throat cancer
mouththroat-about.inShort: Mouth cancer can start on the tongue, gums, lips or inside the cheeks. Cancer in the part of the throat just behind the mouth is called oropharyngeal cancer.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Mouth cancer can start on the tongue, gums, lips or inside the cheeks. Cancer in the part of the throat just behind the mouth is called oropharyngeal cancer.
Mouth cancer mostly affects older adults. In Finland the average age at diagnosis is 69. In the UK, most people are diagnosed between 65 and 70.
In Finland, men are diagnosed a little more often than women. Cases have been rising. Tongue cancer has increased in people under 45 in some Western countries.
Throat cancer behind the mouth that is linked to HPV tends to affect younger people. These people usually do not smoke and drink little or no alcohol.

list: Finland: about 400 mouth cancers (tongue, lip and other mouth lining) are found each year.
Finland, 2023: about 8 new mouth cancers per 100,000 men and 5 per 100,000 women a year. Cases have been rising.
Finland: the average age when mouth cancer is found is 69 (men 66, women 71).
Finland, diagnosed 2021 to 2024: 64% of men and 74% of women with mouth cancer are alive five years later (relative survival).
Finland: almost 90% of mouth cancers start on the edge of the tongue (51%), the gums (21%) or the floor of the mouth (15%).
Finland: in one Finnish study, 57% of people with mouth cancer had a history of smoking or heavy drinking.
Finland: smokers have about 6 times the risk of mouth cancer. For people who both smoke and drink heavily, the risk is 15 to 30 times higher.
Smoking or other tobacco use, including breathing other people's smoke
Alcohol. Smoking and drinking together raise the risk many times over.
Chewing tobacco, betel nut or paan
Patches in the mouth that can turn into cancer: white patches (leukoplakia), red patches (erythroplakia), and oral lichen planus
Poor mouth hygiene and severe gum disease (periodontitis)
HPV infection: a major factor for cancer in the throat behind the mouth (tonsils, back of the tongue). The Finnish guideline says it is not a factor for cancer inside the mouth
Sun on the lips from outdoor work or sunbeds (lip cancer)
A weakened immune system, for example from HIV or from medicines taken after an organ transplant
Having had cancer before, or a brother or sister who had head and neck cancer
Some people have no known risk factor
Avoid tobacco and alcohol. This is the most important step. The risk drops fairly quickly after you stop smoking and heavy drinking.
Keep your mouth clean and go to regular dental check-ups. The dentist checks the lining of your mouth.
Eat plenty of vegetables, fruit and fish. Coffee and tea may also lower risk, but the evidence is weaker.
Do not chew tobacco, betel nut or paan.
Cut down on processed meat, red meat, and foods high in fat, sugar and salt. Exercise regularly.
Cut down on alcohol.

p: See a dentist or doctor about any mouth change that has not gone away in 2 to 3 weeks. Examples are a sore, a red or white patch, or a lump. Others are ongoing pain, trouble swallowing or speaking, a hoarse voice that stays, or a lump in the neck or throat. A dentist can check your mouth too. A neck lump can be a sign of a more advanced cancer. Tests and treatment are then always urgent. In Finland, a yearly mouth check is advised for some people. These are people over 40 who smoke or drink heavily, or who have risky patches in the mouth. Early mouth cancer often causes few symptoms, so regular dental visits matter.
A dentist or doctor looks inside your mouth and feels your mouth and neck. Mouth cancer can be spotted at an ordinary mouth check or dental visit.
A small tissue sample (biopsy) is taken, usually with local anaesthetic, and looked at under a microscope. In Finland the diagnosis is always based on this tissue sample.
If cancer is found, MRI or CT scans (sometimes ultrasound, PET-CT or a jaw X-ray) show how far it has spread. The neck lymph glands are always checked, because mouth cancer can spread there early.
For throat cancer behind the mouth, a thin camera tube is passed through the nose (nasoendoscopy). The biopsy is tested for HPV. No blood test can diagnose mouth or throat cancer.

Surgery is the most common treatment for mouth cancer. It may include removing lymph glands in the neck. Sometimes part of the tongue or jaw is removed too. Skin or bone from elsewhere in the body may be used to rebuild the area.

Radiotherapy is added after surgery when needed, sometimes together with chemotherapy (chemoradiotherapy). In Finland it usually lasts about 6 to 7 weeks. In the UK, radiotherapy alone may be enough for a cancer found early.

Targeted medicines or immunotherapy are sometimes used if the cancer has spread or come back. In Finland a university hospital team plans treatment. Mouth infections and badly damaged teeth are treated first.

Finland has no national screening programme for mouth or throat cancer. Finland's national programmes are only for breast, cervical and colorectal cancer. The Finnish guideline says there is little evidence that screening the whole population lowers deaths from mouth cancer. Instead, the lining of the mouth is checked at regular dental visits. A yearly check is advised for some people. These are people over 40 who smoke or drink heavily, or who have risky patches in the mouth.

pancreas-about.title: Pancreas cancer: the basics
pancreas-about.inShort: Pancreatic cancer starts in the pancreas, an organ high up in your tummy that helps with digestion and makes hormones such as insulin. It often causes no early symptoms, so it is usually found late.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Pancreatic cancer starts in the pancreas, an organ high up in your tummy that helps with digestion and makes hormones such as insulin. It often causes no early symptoms, so it is usually found late.
Pancreatic cancer can affect anyone, but it becomes more likely after age 65. It is not common under 40.
In Finland, about 1,200 people are diagnosed each year, in roughly equal numbers of women and men. The peak age is about 70.
In the UK, almost half of new cases are in people aged 75 or older.

list: Finland: about 1,200 new pancreatic cancers are found each year (596 in women and 597 in men in 2020).
Finland: it is most common around age 70, but it can also happen in younger people.
Finland: only about 5 in 100 people with pancreatic cancer are alive 5 years after diagnosis. The page's survival figures cover people diagnosed around 2011 to 2013.
Finland: an operation that removes all the cancer is possible in about 15 to 30 in 100 cases.
Europe (ESMO patient guide): the average age at diagnosis is 71 years for men and 75 years for women.
UK: almost half of all new cases are in people aged 75 and over, and it is very rare under age 40.
UK: more than 15 in 100 pancreatic cancers (over 15%) are caused by smoking.
Being older, especially over 65
Smoking
Being overweight or obese
Long-term swelling of the pancreas (chronic pancreatitis)
Diabetes (the cancer can also sometimes cause diabetes)
A family history of pancreatic cancer, or certain inherited gene changes such as BRCA2
Eating a lot of red or processed meat (the evidence is weaker)
Drinking a lot of alcohol over many years (the evidence is weaker)
Stop smoking. After about 20 years without smoking, the risk is the same as for people who never smoked.
Reach and keep a healthy weight.
Eat less red and processed meat, for example ham, bacon or salami.
Drink less alcohol. The European Code says to avoid alcohol.
Pancreatic cancer cannot always be prevented, so get any symptoms checked even if you have no risk factors.

p: Ask for an urgent appointment if you notice yellow skin or yellow whites of the eyes. Do the same if you have been sick for over 2 days or have had diarrhoea for over 7 days. Also see a doctor if you lose a lot of weight without trying. Do so too if symptoms get worse or last more than 2 weeks. Many of these symptoms have other causes, but finding cancer early may make it easier to treat.
Scans come first. A CT scan is the most common test to find a tumour. Ultrasound, MRI or PET scans may be used as well.
Doctors may take a small sample of tissue (a biopsy) to check for cancer cells. Sometimes this is done with a thin tube passed through the mouth into the stomach.
Blood tests are used too. A marker called CA 19-9 can be high in pancreatic cancer, but it can also be high in other conditions. It is not enough on its own.

Sometimes doctors also use a small operation to look inside your tummy (laparoscopy). Another option is an X-ray test of the pancreas done through a tube passed down from the mouth (ERCP). Sometimes the cancer is only found during surgery.
Surgery to remove the cancer is the only treatment that can cure it. It is possible only in some people, often because the cancer has already spread when it is found.
Chemotherapy is used before or after surgery, or on its own when surgery is not possible. Radiotherapy is used less often, usually together with chemotherapy.
Supportive care helps with pain, sickness, tiredness, weight loss and digestion. If the cancer cannot be cured, a palliative care team helps keep you comfortable.

Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and bowel cancer, so pancreatic cancer is not in a national programme. The UK has no national screening for it either, because the cancer is fairly uncommon and the benefits would not outweigh the costs. Some people at high risk may be offered tests, sometimes as part of research. Examples are people with certain inherited gene changes or several close relatives with the cancer.

liver-about.title: Liver cancer: the basics
liver-about.inShort: Primary liver cancer starts in the liver, a large organ on the upper right side of your tummy. In Finland it is fairly rare, and it usually grows in a liver already damaged by cirrhosis or another long-term liver disease.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Primary liver cancer starts in the liver, a large organ on the upper right side of your tummy. In Finland it is fairly rare, and it usually grows in a liver already damaged by cirrhosis or another long-term liver disease.
Primary liver cancer can affect anyone. It is more likely after age 60, and men get it more often than women.
In Finland, new cases are most common around age 70, and about two in three people with the common type (HCC) are men.
More than 9 in 10 people with HCC in Finland already have liver damage, for example from cirrhosis.
In the UK, most people diagnosed are over 60, and the highest rates are at ages 85 to 89.

list: Finland 2020: 227 new cancers that started in the liver in women and 501 in men.
Finland: about 320 new cases a year are hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the most common type that starts in liver tissue.
Finland: more than 90 in 100 people with HCC (over 90%) have a liver already damaged by cirrhosis or another long-term liver disease.
Finland: new cases are most common around age 70, and about two in three people with HCC are men.
Finland: surgery to remove the cancer is possible in only about 15 to 30 in 100 cases.
Finland: the Finnish Cancer Society lists liver cancer, with lung, gallbladder and pancreatic cancer, among the cancers that are still very hard to cure.
UK: smoking causes 20 in 100 liver cancers (20%), overweight and obesity more than 20 in 100, and alcohol 7 in 100 (7%).
Cirrhosis (scarring of the liver)
Long-term hepatitis B, C or D infection
Drinking a lot of alcohol over many years (in Finland, alcohol-related liver damage is the most common cause)
Fatty liver disease, which is linked to being overweight and to diabetes
Diabetes
Being overweight or obese
Smoking
Contact with some chemicals at work, such as vinyl chloride and arsenic
A parent, brother or sister who had primary liver cancer
HIV, gallstones, or liver flukes (a parasite that is not common in the UK)
Get the hepatitis B vaccine. A vaccine at birth can remove hepatitis B as a risk factor.
If you have hepatitis B or C, get tested and treated early. This can help prevent liver cancer.
Drink less alcohol. The European Code says to avoid alcohol.
Reach and keep a healthy weight.
Stop smoking.
Use protective clothing and a mask if your work involves harmful chemicals.
Liver cancer cannot always be prevented, so get any symptoms checked.

p: Ask for an urgent appointment if you notice yellow skin or yellow whites of the eyes. Do the same if you have been sick for over 2 days. See a doctor if you feel a lump in your tummy or lose much weight without meaning to. Also go if your symptoms get worse. If you already have cirrhosis, tell your doctor about any new or worsening symptoms. Early liver cancer often causes no symptoms at all.
A doctor may examine your tummy and chest. You will usually have blood tests that show how well your liver works.
A blood marker called AFP is raised in up to 80 in 100 people with HCC. It is not raised in everyone, so a blood test alone cannot give the diagnosis.
Scans find the tumour. Ultrasound, CT or MRI are used. CT or MRI often give the answer, so a biopsy (a small tissue sample) is often not needed.
More scans, and sometimes a small keyhole operation (laparoscopy), show how far the cancer has spread.
If the cancer is small and has not spread, surgery to remove part of the liver may be possible. Some people with early cancer may be offered a liver transplant.
If surgery is not possible, doctors can destroy the tumour with heat (thermal ablation). They can also treat it through the blood vessels that feed it, or use radiotherapy.
Targeted medicines and immunotherapy are used for cancer that cannot be removed or has spread. In Finland, ordinary chemotherapy has not proved effective for this cancer.

Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and bowel cancer, so liver cancer is not in a national programme. The UK has none either, because liver cancer is rare, no suitable test exists and screening would cost a lot. People at high risk may be offered an ultrasound scan every 6 months, sometimes with an AFP blood test. This includes people with cirrhosis or long-term hepatitis B. Advice differs: European guidelines (EASL, ESMO) back 6-monthly ultrasound for people with cirrhosis. The Finnish Terveyskirjasto article says regular scans for all people with cirrhosis have not been shown to change treatment or results.

kidney-about.title: Kidney cancer: the basics
kidney-about.inShort: Kidney cancer starts in the kidneys, the two organs that clean waste and extra fluid out of your blood and turn it into pee. About 1,000 people in Finland are diagnosed each year, and many cases are found by chance on an ultrasound done for another reason.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Kidney cancer starts in the kidneys, the two organs that clean waste and extra fluid out of your blood and turn it into pee. About 1,000 people in Finland are diagnosed each year, and many cases are found by chance on an ultrasound done for another reason.
Most people with kidney cancer are over 60, though younger people can get it too. Men are affected more often than women.
In Finland, 1,032 people were diagnosed in 2022: 643 men and 389 women. The usual age when it is found is 60 to 70.
In the UK, around 35 in 100 kidney cancers are found in people aged 75 and over.

list: Finland 2022: 1,032 new kidney cancers were found, 643 in men and 389 in women.
Finland: people are usually between 60 and 70 years old when kidney cancer is found.
Finland: new cases in women have stayed level since the 1990s but have risen in men in recent years. Deaths have fallen in both since the 1970s.
Finland: most kidney cancers are found by chance on an ultrasound done for another reason.
Finland: nearly 70 in 100 people with kidney cancer are alive 5 years after diagnosis. For small cancers found by chance, up to 95 in 100 are alive after 5 years.
Finland: a little over 1 in 4 people already have spread of the cancer when it is found.
UK: around 35 in 100 kidney cancers (35%) are found in people aged 75 and over.
Smoking (the most important single risk factor named in Finland)
Being overweight or obese
High blood pressure
A close relative with kidney cancer
Rare inherited conditions, such as von Hippel-Lindau disease or tuberous sclerosis
Long-term dialysis, or long-term kidney disease
Men who have had kidney stones
Earlier radiotherapy, or working with certain chemicals (both uncommon)
Stop smoking. After 10 years without smoking, the risk is close to that of people who never smoked.
Lose weight if you are overweight.
If you have high blood pressure, eat less salt and cut down on alcohol and caffeine.
Kidney cancer cannot always be prevented, so get any symptoms checked even if you have no risk factors.

p: Ask for an urgent appointment if your pee smells bad, looks cloudy or contains blood. Do the same if peeing hurts, or you need to pee suddenly or more often. Also go urgently for a pain in the back below the ribs that will not go away. The same goes for pain in the genitals, or a lump or swelling in the back, below the ribs or on the neck. These signs can look like a kidney infection, which can become serious without fast treatment. See a doctor too if you lose a noticeable amount of weight, have a fever that will not go away, or feel extremely tired.
Kidney cancer is often found by chance on an ultrasound done for another reason. If it is suspected, you usually have an ultrasound scan and a CT scan.
A CT scan of the chest and tummy shows the size and position of the tumour and whether it has spread. A needle biopsy of the kidney may be done, which can help when a lump might be harmless.
Sometimes a camera is passed through the urethra to look inside the bladder (cystoscopy).
If cancer is found, an MRI scan, a chest X-ray or a bone scan may show how far it has spread (the stage).

Surgery is the main treatment and the only one that can cure kidney cancer. Doctors remove the whole kidney or, if possible, only the part with the cancer. In Finland, most operations are keyhole operations.

If the cancer is small and surgery is not suitable, doctors can freeze it (cryotherapy) or heat it with radio waves (radiofrequency ablation). European urologists also list active surveillance and a type of radiotherapy called SBRT as options when the cancer is still inside the kidney.

For cancer that has spread or comes back, targeted medicines and immunotherapy are the main drug treatments. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are used less often. After surgery, Finnish doctors say extra treatment has not been shown to lower the chance of the cancer returning, so you have check-ups.

Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and bowel cancer, so kidney cancer is not in a national programme. The UK has no national screening for it either, and many kidney cancers are found by chance on a scan done for another reason. People from families with rare inherited conditions may be offered a yearly ultrasound or MRI scan of the kidneys. One example is von Hippel-Lindau disease.

bladder-about.title: Bladder cancer: the basics
bladder-about.inShort: Bladder cancer starts in the bladder, the organ that stores your pee. Smoking is its main risk factor, and blood in the pee is the most common warning sign.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Bladder cancer starts in the bladder, the organ that stores your pee. Smoking is its main risk factor, and blood in the pee is the most common warning sign.
Bladder cancer is more common in men, and in people over 60.
In Finland, about 1,500 people get bladder cancer each year, and 75 in 100 of them are men. It is the fourth most common cancer in men. It is most often found at ages 75 to 79.
The European ESMO guide also says most new cases are in people aged 75 and older.

list: Finland: about 1,500 new bladder cancers are found each year, and 75 in 100 of them are in men.
Finland: it is the fourth most common cancer in men, and it is most often found at ages 75 to 79.
Finland: smoking raises the risk of bladder cancer 4 to 10 times.
Finland: 75 to 80 in 100 bladder cancers are still only in the bladder lining when found.
Finland: 5 years after diagnosis, 75 in 100 men and 70 in 100 women are alive (Cancer Registry figures quoted by Terveyskirjasto).
Europe (ESMO patient guide): smoking accounts for around half of bladder cancers. People who smoke have four times the risk of people who never smoked.
UK: 80 in 100 people with bladder cancer (80%) have some blood in their pee.
Smoking or using chewing tobacco (the main risk factor)
Being a man, and being over 60
Working with certain chemicals, for example in the dye, rubber, textile or oil industries (now a small cause in Finland)
Long-term bladder irritation, for example from repeated urine infections, bladder stones or a catheter left in for a long time
Radiotherapy to the pelvis for an earlier cancer
Being overweight, or having diabetes
A close relative who had bladder cancer
An infection called schistosomiasis (bilharzia), found in parts of Africa and Asia
Stop smoking. Quitting lowers your risk compared with carrying on.
Lose weight if you are overweight.
Use protective clothing and a mask if your work involves harmful chemicals, and follow safety rules at work.
Bladder cancer cannot always be prevented, so get any symptoms checked.

p: See a doctor if you ever notice blood in your pee. That applies even if it is a small amount, happens only once, or you have no other symptoms. NHS advice is to ask for an urgent appointment. Finnish doctors (Duodecim) say visible blood in the pee always needs tests. Get help at once if peeing becomes difficult, and otherwise on the next working day. Burning or needing to pee often is usually an infection, but if it lasts or keeps coming back, you need more tests.
Your doctor will check you and ask for a urine sample. You may also have a blood test, or an examination through the back passage or vagina.

The main test is a cystoscopy. A thin tube with a camera goes through the urethra into the bladder so the doctor can look inside. You may feel some discomfort, but it should not hurt. A small tissue sample (biopsy) can be taken at the same time.
Doctors usually then remove the tumour, or part of it, through the urethra in an operation called TURBT. The lab checks the type and how deep it has grown.

A urine test for cancer cells finds only about 1 in 3 bladder cancers, so a normal result does not rule cancer out. Ultrasound, CT or MRI scans, and sometimes a bone scan, show if the cancer has spread.

Surgery is the main treatment. Cancer that is only in the bladder lining is removed through the urethra (TURBT). Medicine is often washed into the bladder afterwards, either chemotherapy or BCG, to lower the chance of the cancer coming back.

Cancer that has grown into the bladder muscle usually needs the whole bladder removed, often with chemotherapy first. Radiotherapy, usually with chemotherapy, can be used instead of surgery for some people. After the bladder is removed, doctors make a new way for you to pass urine.
If the cancer has spread, chemotherapy and immunotherapy are the main treatments. Bladder cancer often comes back, so you need regular check-ups, which may include a cystoscopy.

Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and bowel cancer, so bladder cancer is not in a national programme. The UK has none either, because no test reliably finds bladder cancer early and the benefits would not outweigh the costs. Testing urine for blood is not a useful screening test for the general population, because small amounts of blood can have other causes. The best way to find bladder cancer early is to see a doctor about any bladder symptoms.

ovary-about.title: Ovary cancer: the basics
ovary-about.inShort: Ovarian cancer starts in the ovaries, two small organs that hold a woman's eggs and make female hormones. Early signs are vague, so it is often found late.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Ovarian cancer starts in the ovaries, two small organs that hold a woman's eggs and make female hormones. Early signs are vague, so it is often found late.
Anyone who has ovaries can develop ovarian cancer. It mostly affects women over 50, and the risk rises with age.
In Finland, about 500 women get it each year. It is most often found at ages 60 to 64, but younger women can be affected too.
Most ovarian cancers start in cells on the surface of the ovary (epithelial cancer). Others start in different tissue inside the ovary.
Cancers that start in the fallopian tubes or the lining of the belly (peritoneum) behave in a similar way. They are often grouped with ovarian cancer.
It can still happen after the ovaries have been taken out, because the tubes or belly lining can be affected.

list: Finland: about 500 women are diagnosed with ovarian cancer each year.
Finland: ovarian cancer is the 10th most common cancer in women.
Finland: it is found most often in women aged 60 to 64, but young women can get it too.
Finland: in about 80% of cases the cancer has already spread widely in the belly or to other organs when it is found.
Finland: 48% of women with ovarian cancer are alive 5 years after diagnosis.
Finland: only 15% of all growths on the ovaries are cancer. Most are not.
Finland: an inherited risk is linked to an estimated 5 to 10% of ovarian cancers.
Getting older
An inherited gene change, such as BRCA1, BRCA2 or the gene change behind Lynch syndrome
A close relative who has had ovarian cancer
Having had breast cancer or bowel cancer in the past
Endometriosis
Diabetes
Being overweight
Smoking (it raises the risk of some types)
Using menopause hormone treatment (HRT). The extra risk is small, and Finnish experts say it falls after you stop
Starting periods young, going through menopause late (after 55), or never having had a baby
Never having used hormonal birth control, such as the pill
Infertility, or having a first baby late in life
Radiotherapy for an earlier cancer
Work that exposed you to asbestos
Stop smoking, if you smoke.
Keep to a healthy weight.
Taking the combined birth control pill lowers the risk. The longer you take it, the more the risk drops.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding both lower the risk.
If ovarian cancer runs in your family, ask a doctor about genetic counselling.
