In Finland, women in BRCA or Lynch syndrome families are advised to have ovaries and tubes removed after having children, or by age 40.
Ovarian cancer cannot always be prevented, so still get symptoms checked.

p: See a doctor if you have any of these symptoms, especially if they are new for you, keep coming back, or get worse. They are common and often have other causes, but checking early matters. Tell the doctor if ovarian or breast cancer runs in your family. In the UK, a doctor who suspects cancer may arrange an urgent referral, usually within 2 weeks. This does not mean you definitely have cancer. Unusual vaginal bleeding, including bleeding after menopause, is one of the signs to get checked.
The doctor asks about your symptoms and your family history. You may have a blood test for a protein called CA125. If it is high, you have an ultrasound scan of the belly and pelvis.
A specialist may then order a CT scan and take a small sample of cells or fluid with a needle. In Finland, other blood markers (HE4, AFP, CA19-9) can also be checked.
Sometimes a thin camera is put into the belly through a small cut (laparoscopy). A scan can miss small ovaries, especially after menopause.
In Finland, the final diagnosis and how far the cancer has spread are usually confirmed during surgery, done at a university hospital. MRI or PET-CT can add information about spread.

Surgery is the main treatment. The surgeon removes as much cancer as possible. In Finland, this usually means both ovaries and tubes, the womb, and fatty tissue in the belly. Early cancers may need less surgery.
Chemotherapy (medicine that kills cancer cells) is given before or after surgery, or on its own. Other options are targeted medicines, radiotherapy and, rarely, hormone treatment.
The plan depends on the cancer type, where it is, whether it has spread, and your health. In Finland, about half of ovarian cancers can be treated with the aim of a cure.

There is no national screening programme for ovarian cancer in the UK, because no test finds it reliably at an early stage. A large UK trial found that ultrasound and the CA125 blood test did not save lives when used as screening. The Cancer Society of Finland also says no method exists to detect the disease early. Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and colorectal cancer. People at high inherited risk (for example BRCA gene changes) can talk to a doctor about their options, which may include preventive surgery.

womb-about.title: Womb cancer: the basics
womb-about.inShort: Womb cancer, also called endometrial cancer, usually starts in the lining of the womb. It is most common after menopause and is often found early because it causes bleeding.

sections.h: What it is and who gets it
p: Womb cancer, also called endometrial cancer, usually starts in the lining of the womb. It is most common after menopause and is often found early because it causes bleeding.
Womb cancer is most common in women who have been through menopause. Anyone who has a womb can get it.
In Finland, about 900 new cases are found each year. Most are in women over 50, and it is rare under 40.
Most womb cancers start in the womb lining (the endometrium). A rarer type starts in the muscle wall of the womb and is called a sarcoma.
You cannot get womb cancer if your womb has been removed (hysterectomy).

Finland: womb cancer is the 4th most common cancer in women.
Finland: about 90% of new cases are in women over 50, and about 50% are in women over 65.
Finland: womb cancer is rare in women under 40.
Finland: 82% of women with womb cancer are alive 5 years after diagnosis.
Finland: when bleeding after menopause keeps happening or returns, the cause is cervical or womb cancer in about 30 to 50% of cases.
UK source: most women diagnosed have been through menopause and are aged 75 to 79.
Being overweight or obese. This is the biggest risk you can change.
Having a lot of the hormone oestrogen in your body over the years
Using oestrogen-only menopause hormone treatment (HRT) without progesterone added
Never having given birth
Starting periods young, or going through menopause late (after 55)
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
Diabetes
A thickened womb lining (endometrial hyperplasia)
Taking tamoxifen for a long time (a breast cancer medicine)
Radiotherapy to the pelvis in the past
A family history of bowel, ovarian or womb cancer
Lynch syndrome, an inherited gene condition
Getting older
Keep to a healthy weight.
Stay active and exercise regularly.
Eat a healthy, balanced diet.
If you want menopause hormone treatment and still have your womb, ask a doctor which type suits you. In Finland, progesterone is added to oestrogen to protect the womb lining.
Having children and taking the combined birth control pill are both linked to a lower risk.
If you have Lynch syndrome, your care team will discuss how to lower your risk. In Finland, this includes yearly check-ups, and removing the womb and ovaries may be considered at age 40 to 50.

p: See a doctor as soon as you notice any of these symptoms. Do not wait, and try not to feel embarrassed. Doctors and nurses are used to talking about them. Bleeding after menopause needs checking. If you take tamoxifen, tell your doctor about any unexpected bleeding. Tell the doctor if you or your family have had cancer or Lynch syndrome. In the UK, a doctor who suspects cancer may arrange an urgent referral. This does not definitely mean you have cancer.
The doctor asks about your health and does a pelvic exam. A scan with a thin probe placed in the vagina (transvaginal ultrasound) shows how thick the womb lining is.

If you have had bleeding, or the lining is thicker than normal, a small sample of the lining is taken (a biopsy). In Finland, this is often done during a clinic visit. A thin camera test of the womb (hysteroscopy) may also be used.
The cervical smear test (Pap test) does not find womb cancer.
If cancer is found, scans such as CT, MRI or PET and a chest X-ray show how far it has spread. Genetic tests can check for Lynch syndrome.
Surgery is usually the main treatment. In Finland, the womb, ovaries and tubes are removed. Lymph nodes may also be removed or sampled. Surgery can be keyhole, robot-assisted or open.
After surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy or both may be added, depending on the chance that the cancer will come back. These can also be the main treatment if surgery is not possible.

Hormone therapy and immunotherapy are options for advanced cancer or cancer that has returned. In Finland, most womb cancers can be treated with the aim of cure. Some young women with a low-risk early type who want children can be offered fertility-sparing treatment.

There is no national screening programme for womb cancer in the UK, because no test can pick it up early. A vaginal ultrasound or womb biopsy has not been shown to work in women without symptoms. Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and colorectal cancer, and the cervical smear does not find womb cancer. For women with Lynch syndrome, UK doctors may offer yearly checks from age 35. Finnish guidance also suggests yearly follow-up from age 35, with a sample of the womb lining.

prevention-code.title: The European Code Against Cancer
prevention-code.inShort: The European Code Against Cancer lists 14 things you can do to lower your risk. It was made by the World Health Organization’s cancer agency for the European Union.

p: The Code is the 5th edition, made by IARC and WHO for the European Commission. It was first published on 6 August 2025. It is written for people living in the European Union.
The Code states that about 40% of cancers can be prevented.

list: 1. Do not smoke or use tobacco. Avoid every form of tobacco and vaping, and quit if you smoke.
2. Keep tobacco smoke away from you. Make sure nobody smokes in your home or car.
3. Avoid or manage excess weight. Eat less high-calorie, sugary, fatty, salty and ultra-processed food, and drink mostly water or unsweetened drinks.
4. Be active. Move more in daily life and spend less time sitting.
5. Eat a healthy diet. Eat plenty of whole grains, vegetables, legumes and fruit, less red meat, and no processed meat.
6. Avoid alcohol. The advice is to stay away from alcoholic drinks.
7. Breastfeed. If you have a baby, breastfeed for as long as you can.
8. Protect yourself from the sun. Limit sun exposure, most of all for children. Use sun protection and never use sunbeds.
9. Know the cancer risks at work. Find out about cancer-causing things at your workplace, ask your employer to protect you and follow safety rules.
10. Check for radon gas at home. Look at a local radon map, then get a professional to measure radon in your home and reduce it if needed.
11. Cut your exposure to air pollution. Walk, cycle or use public transport, choose low-traffic routes, and avoid burning coal or wood at home.
12. Get vaccinated and tested for cancer-causing infections. Vaccinate children against hepatitis B and HPV, and take part in recommended testing and treatment for hepatitis, HIV and H. pylori.
13. Be careful with hormone therapy for menopause. If you choose it after talking with a health professional, use it for as short a time as possible.
14. Join organised cancer screening. Take part in the screening programmes your country recommends for bowel, breast, cervical and lung cancer.

p: The Code also has 14 recommendations for policy-makers. They are not listed here.
Finland sets its own screening ages and intervals. Use the national screening pages in this app for them.

what-is-cancer.title: What is cancer?
what-is-cancer.inShort: Cancer is not one disease. It starts when cells grow without proper control. There are more than 200 types.

p: Cancer happens when cells in your body keep growing without proper control.

It begins when changes in a cell's genes damage the controls on how it grows and divides. One change is usually not enough. The body usually repairs this kind of damage, but if repair fails, damaged cells can divide without control.

A group of abnormal cells can form a lump called a tumour. A benign tumour stays in one place, grows slowly and does not usually cause death. A malignant (cancerous) tumour grows faster, does not stay in one place and is often life-threatening. Some cancers, such as leukaemia, do not form a lump at all.
Cancer cells can travel through the blood or the lymph system and start new tumours in other organs. These new tumours are called metastases, or secondary cancer.
Cancer is not one disease. There are more than 200 types, and their causes and behaviour differ a lot.
If symptoms are caused by cancer, finding it early may make it easier to treat. So it is important to get unusual symptoms checked by a doctor.
The stage of a cancer tells how far it has grown and spread.
Doctors often use the TNM system. T is the size of the main tumour. N is whether it has spread to nearby lymph nodes. M is whether it has spread to other parts of the body (distant metastases).
The result is a stage from 0 to IV. Stage 0 is a small cancer that has not spread (carcinoma in situ). Stage IV means the cancer has spread widely. Some stages have sub-groups.

Stage is not the same as grade. Grade shows how much the cancer cells look like normal cells from the same tissue. Cells that look less normal are called poorly differentiated, and these tumours tend to spread more easily.

breast.name: Breast
breast.blurb: Ages 50–69 are invited. Changes to look for.
breast.lede: About 5,000 women in Finland are diagnosed each year. More than half are in the screening age group, 50–69.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: New lump or swelling
items.what: A new lump or swollen patch on the breast, near the collarbone, or in the armpit.

items.title: Skin like orange peel
items.what: Skin that looks dimpled or pitted, a little like the surface of an orange. It may feel different too.

items.title: Small dimple where skin pulls in
items.what: A little dent in the skin, like a dimple, where the skin seems pulled inwards.

items.title: Red or darker skin
items.what: The breast skin looks red on white skin, or darker than usual on brown or black skin. It may look inflamed.

items.title: Breast size or shape changes
items.what: One or both breasts look bigger, smaller or a different shape than before. Uneven breasts are common, so look for change.

items.title: Nipple turned inwards
items.what: A nipple that has sunk or been pulled into the breast, when it used to point out.

items.title: Rash on the nipple
items.what: A scaly, itchy rash around or on the nipple, similar to eczema.

items.title: Fluid from the nipple
items.what: Liquid from a nipple when you are not pregnant or breastfeeding. It may have blood in it.

items.title: Non-healing sore or rash
items.what: An open sore or a rash on the breast or nipple that does not heal.

items.title: Tight or hardened area
items.what: An area of the breast that feels tight or thickened.

items.title: Warm, tingly, itchy or sore breast
items.what: A breast that feels hot, prickly, itchy or painful.

items.title: Pain that is nearly always there
items.what: Pain in the breast or armpit that is nearly always there. Pain on its own is not usually cancer.

items.title: Whole breast red, hard and sore
items.what: The whole breast looks inflamed and feels sore or hard, with skin like orange peel. It can feel like an infection.

symptoms.see: See a doctor soon if you find a lump or any change in your breast that is not normal for you. Most lumps are not cancer, but every lump should be checked.
symptoms.note: Many breast changes are not cancer. Cysts and other harmless changes are common. Get any change checked, even right after a screening.
symptoms.contact: Contact your health centre, occupational health clinic or a private clinic. Breast cancer is most common in women. It can also affect men and non-binary people.

check.title: Look and feel for changes
text: The most effective way to find breast cancer early is screening. Between screenings, it helps to know how your breasts normally look and feel, so a change stands out.
You do not need a strict routine. Cancer Research UK finds no good evidence that routine self-checks save lives, and says they can lead to extra tests.

steps.t: Check in bed, in the shower or when you get dressed. A few minutes is enough. If you have periods, check just after one ends, when breasts are softest.

steps.h: Look with arms by your sides
steps.t: Stand at a mirror with your arms relaxed by your sides. Look from the front, then turn and look from each side.
steps.look: Size and shape of each breast. Rash, colour change or sores on the skin or nipple.

steps.h: Raise your arms and look again
steps.t: Lift both arms above your head and look again, from the front and from each side. Also look at the skin under each breast.
steps.look: Any change in size or shape. Rash, colour change or sores.

steps.t: Place your hands on your hips and keep your shoulders straight. Look at both breasts in the mirror.
steps.look: Dimpling, puckering or bulging skin. A nipple that has moved or turned inwards. Redness, rash or swelling.

steps.t: While you are at the mirror, look for any fluid coming from either nipple. It can be watery, milky or yellow, or it can be blood.
steps.look: Fluid from one or both nipples.

steps.h: Lie on your back to feel
steps.t: Lie flat on your back. This spreads the breast out, so it is easier to feel all of it. With large breasts, a pillow under your shoulder can help.
steps.look: Anything that feels new or different from your normal.

steps.h: Use flat fingers in small circles
steps.t: Use the pads of your first few fingers, flat and together. Press in small circles about 2.5 cm (an inch) wide. Use your right hand on the left breast, then swap.
At each spot, press lightly for tissue just under the skin, with medium pressure for the middle, and firmly for deep tissue near the ribs.
steps.look: Any lump or odd area you have not felt before.

steps.t: Cover from your collarbone down to the top of your tummy, and from your armpit across to the centre of your chest. Pick a pattern so you miss nothing: rows like mowing a lawn, or wider rings from the nipple.
steps.look: A lump, a swollen area, or a thick patch anywhere in that zone.

steps.h: Feel standing or in the shower
steps.t: You can also feel your breasts standing up. Wet, slippery skin in the shower helps your fingers glide. Feel each breast with your arm at your side, stretched out, and raised.

steps.h: Feel around each nipple and armpit
steps.t: Feel all around each nipple, and over the top of it too. Then feel the side of your chest and your armpit.
steps.look: Fluid from the nipple, a nipple turning inwards, or a rash on it.

steps.t: If you notice anything new or unusual, make an appointment. Usually the cause is harmless, but it is better to have it checked early.

normal: Breasts can feel smooth or lumpy. Both are normal.
Before a period, breasts often get bigger, tender and lumpy, then settle again once the period ends.
One breast can be larger than the other, or sit higher or lower.
Nipples differ in shape, colour and direction. A nipple that has always been turned inwards is normal for you.
A few hairs around the nipple are normal.
Breasts feel different in pregnancy, while breastfeeding and after menopause.
Three in four changes found in breasts are harmless, such as cysts, fatty lumps or scars.
check.found: Do not wait. See a doctor soon about a new lump, swelling, skin change, nipple change or fluid from a nipple, even if you were screened recently. In Finland, book at your health centre, workplace clinic or a private clinic. Most changes turn out to be harmless, but only tests can tell. Being sent to a breast clinic does not mean you have cancer.

videos.title: How to check your breasts (video by cancer nurse Roz, on the page)

check.differ: Sources differ on how often to check. The NHS and the Irish Cancer Society say about once a month. The Cancer Society of Finland puts screening first. A Cancer Society doctor says routine checks have not been shown to lower deaths and monthly checks are not needed. All agree: know your normal, and see a doctor about any change.

breast.screeningText: In Finland, women aged 50–69 are invited to a mammogram every two years. Invitations go out at even ages, 50 to 68. A national screening group proposed in March 2025 to widen this to ages 46–74. That needed more political decisions, so check the current ages. The European Code advises a mammogram every two years for women aged 50–69, and says to consider ages 45–49 and 70–74.

cervical.name: Cervical
cervical.blurb: Ages 30–65. Home sampling tested in some counties.
cervical.lede: Cervical cancer has precursors that screening can find and treat before cancer develops.
cervical.programme: Cell or HPV test every 5 years, ages 30–65

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Bleeding between periods
items.what: Spotting or bleeding at a time when you are not having a period.

items.title: Bleeding during or after sex
items.what: Blood seen during sex or afterwards. It often has a harmless cause, but it still needs checking.

items.title: Bleeding after menopause
items.what: Any vaginal bleeding after your periods have stopped for good.

items.title: Heavier periods than usual
items.what: Periods that are heavier than is normal for you.

items.title: Change in vaginal discharge
items.what: Discharge that is different from your usual, sometimes with an unpleasant smell.

items.title: Pain during sex
items.what: Discomfort or pain when having sex.

items.title: Pain in lower back or pelvis
items.what: An ache in your lower back, between your hip bones, or low in your tummy.

items.title: Often no symptoms early on
items.what: Early cervical cancer and pre-cancer changes usually cause no symptoms, so screening matters.

symptoms.see: See a doctor if you notice unusual vaginal bleeding or discharge. Early cervical cancer often has no symptoms, so go to screening even when you feel well.

kit.title: Home sampling (2026 study)
kit.text: In some counties you can take the cervical screening sample at home, as part of a study run by Fimlab. You need a screening invitation first.

cervical.screeningText: Finland has run a national cervical cancer screening programme since the 1960s. The screening test is either a Pap test or an HPV test. An unclear or abnormal result may lead to a colposcopy. The European Code advises HPV screening at least five years apart for women aged 30–65. The ages and intervals Finland uses now are not stated on the pages read here, so use the app's Finnish screening sources for them.

bowel.name: Bowel
bowel.blurb: A test you take at home and post.
bowel.lede: Bowel cancer is the third most common cancer in Finland. The screening test is a kit you use at home.
bowel.programme: Home test every 2 years. Invited at 60, 62 … 72 now. All ages 56–74 by 2031.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Blood in poo, red or dark
items.what: Bright red blood with the poo, or poo that looks dark red, black or like tar.

items.title: Bleeding from the bottom
items.what: Bleeding from your back passage.

items.title: Change in your usual poo
items.what: Your poo turns softer, runny or hard to pass in a way that is odd for you, or you go more or less often.

items.title: Still needing to poo
items.what: Often feeling you need to poo, even straight after you have been.

items.title: Tummy pain, bloating or a lump
items.what: Pain or bloating in your tummy, or a lump you can feel there.

items.title: Weight loss without trying
items.what: Losing weight when you are not dieting or trying to.

items.title: Tired and short of breath
items.what: Feeling very tired or out of breath. These can be signs of anaemia caused by bowel cancer.

items.title: Heavy bleeding or large clots
items.what: A lot of blood, large clots, or bleeding that will not stop is an emergency.

items.title: Cramps, bloating and being sick
items.what: Cramping tummy pain, a bloated tummy, constipation with no wind passing, and vomiting can mean a blocked bowel. This is an emergency.

symptoms.see: See a doctor if you notice blood in your stool or a clear change in how your bowels work. Do not wait for a screening invitation. If your belly is very painful, you vomit and no stool passes, go to emergency care straight away.

kit.title: The national home test
kit.text: The bowel screening test is already a home kit. It arrives with your invitation letter. You do not order it.

video.title: Fimlab suolistosyövän seulonta – näin otat näytteen.

bowel.screeningText: Finland started national bowel cancer screening in 2022. People in the invited age groups get an invitation at home every two years. They take a stool sample at home and post it to the lab. The test (called FIT) looks for blood you cannot see. It is free and voluntary. In 2026, people turning 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 70 and 72 are invited. Screening is growing step by step to all 56–74-year-olds. Over 90% of results are normal. The European Code advises a stool test every two years for ages 50–74.

skin.name: Skin
skin.blurb: Know your moles. Sun and UV.
skin.lede: Knowing your moles is the best habit. Check your skin regularly and notice what is normal for you.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Mole with an uneven shape
items.what: Normal moles are round with smooth edges. A melanoma is often lopsided: two halves that do not match, and ragged edges.

items.title: Mole with several colours
items.what: Normal moles are one colour. A melanoma can mix two or more colours, such as brown and black.

items.title: Mole that looks large
items.what: Most normal moles are no bigger than the end of a pencil. Melanomas are often wider than 6 mm.

items.title: Mole that changes over time
items.what: A mole that grows, or changes shape or colour. It may also feel itchy or sore, bleed, or form a crust.

items.title: New odd mark that stays
items.what: A new or unusual mark that is still there after a few weeks. This includes marks on the palms and soles.

items.title: Dark patch under a nail
items.what: A dark area under a fingernail or toenail that did not come from a knock or injury.

items.title: One mole that looks different
items.what: One mole stands out from all your others. Your moles should look fairly alike, so a new odd one is the 'ugly duckling'.

items.title: Pink or red bump (basal cell)
items.what: A slow-growing pink or red bump with tiny blood vessels. It may form a sore in the middle, with a pearly, beaded edge.

items.title: Flat red patch (basal cell)
items.what: A flat red patch with a sharp border and a thin thread-like edge. It may have small sores and scabs.

items.title: Crusted sore (squamous cell)
items.what: A rough crust over a raw sore, often on sun-exposed skin or the lower lip. It may bleed and grows faster than basal cell.

items.title: Red scaly sun spot (pre-cancer)
items.what: A round, red patch that is sometimes flaky. It can look like eczema at first, and it can turn into squamous cell cancer.

items.title: A sore that will not heal
items.what: A sore or broken patch of skin that bleeds, keeps scabbing over, or heals and then comes back.

items.title: Darker patch on darker skin
items.what: On brown or black skin, a patch may look darker than the skin around it, rather than red.

symptoms.see: See a doctor if a mole changes size, shape or colour, or is painful, itchy, inflamed, bleeding or crusty. Also go if a new or odd mark has not gone away after a few weeks, or a sore does not heal. Do not wait because a spot is painless, as not all skin cancers hurt. If you notice two or more warning signs, do not delay. In Finland, the 'VARO' check lists four warning signs: uneven colour, a width over 6 mm, an irregular edge, and uneven halves. Show any such mole to a doctor. Small dark dots appearing around a mole are always a sign of melanoma. To check hard-to-see areas, use a mirror or ask a friend or partner. Photos with a ruler next to the spot help you notice changes. The doctor may photograph the mole to send to a skin specialist.
symptoms.note: If a mole has changed or a new, different one appears, see your doctor.
symptoms.contact: A doctor diagnoses skin cancer by examining a tissue sample.

check.title: Check your skin
text: Regular checking is the best way to learn about the moles on your skin. Use a mirror for areas you cannot see.

steps.t: Use one big mirror that shows your whole body, plus a small hand mirror. Check front and back, and take extra care with skin the sun reaches.
steps.look: New moles, or spots that changed in size, colour or shape.

steps.t: Check your face, including nose, lips and mouth. Check behind and around each ear. Part your hair with a comb to see your scalp.
steps.look: Rough or scaly patches (you can feel these before you see them) and sores that do not heal.

steps.t: Look at both sides of each hand, and between the fingers. Look at your fingernails and toenails.
steps.look: A dark area under a nail that did not come from an injury.

steps.t: Check the front of your neck and your chest. Look between and under your breasts if you have them.
Bend your elbow to see your upper arm, and check your armpits.

steps.h: Hand mirror for neck and back
steps.t: Hold the small mirror up to see the back of your neck and your whole back.
Look at your bottom and the backs of your legs. End with the soles of your feet, then each gap between your toes.
Asymmetry, Border, Colour, Diameter, Evolving. One sign alone is not a diagnosis. A mole that shows any of them is worth showing to a doctor.
Compare your moles with each other. A mole that looks different from the rest is called the “ugly duckling”. Have it examined.
steps.look: A mole that stands out, or looks much darker than your others.

steps.t: Take a photo of any spot that looks wrong, with a ruler or tape measure beside it. Photos show size and make changes easier to spot.
If a mole has changed, or a new one appears that looks different, see your doctor.

check.found: If a mole has changed, or a new one appears that looks different, see your doctor. Skin cancer is diagnosed from a tissue sample.

videos.title: How To Recognise Symptoms of Melanoma (video on the skin-check page)

check.differ: No national guidance on how often to check your skin was found in these sources. They say to check regularly and to know your skin.

abcde.t: The two halves of the spot are different shapes or sizes. A normal mole looks similar on both halves.
Edges look blurry or jagged. A normal mole has a smooth, regular edge.
More than one shade in the same spot, such as black, brown and pink. A normal mole is usually one even colour.
Wider than about 6 mm. Normal moles are about the size of a pencil end or smaller. Early melanomas can be smaller.
The spot changes over time: it grows, changes shape or shifts colour. It may also bleed, itch, feel different or turn crusty.

skin.screeningText: Finland has no national skin cancer screening programme. Its national programmes cover only breast, cervical and colorectal cancer. In the UK, there is no national melanoma screening programme (Cancer Research UK). Research has not shown that the benefits outweigh the risks. The best way to find melanoma early is to know the signs and see a doctor if you notice any. People at higher risk can have skin checks by a specialist. Euromelanoma advises checking your skin for changes, using the ABCDE signs and the 'ugly duckling' sign.

prostate.name: Prostate
prostate.blurb: The signs to know, and when to talk to your health centre.
prostate.lede: Know the signs, and talk to your health centre if something changes.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Often nothing at first
items.what: Early prostate cancer usually causes no signs. It grows at the edge of the gland, away from the tube that carries pee.

items.title: Weak or stop-start pee flow
items.what: Pee comes out in a weak stream, or it stops and starts. You may struggle to get going or have to strain.

items.title: Peeing often, even at night
items.what: You need the toilet more often than usual, sometimes in a hurry, and you get up to pee during the night.

items.title: Feeling you have not finished
items.what: Right after peeing, it still feels as if your bladder is not empty.

items.title: Blood in pee or semen
items.what: You see blood in your pee or in your semen.

items.title: Trouble with erections
items.what: You cannot get or keep an erection, which is new for you.

items.title: Lower back, hip or pelvis pain
items.what: An ache in the lower back, pelvis or hips. When prostate cancer spreads, it often goes to the bones first.

items.title: Weight loss without trying
items.what: Losing weight when you are not dieting can be a sign of advanced prostate cancer.

symptoms.see: See a doctor if you have trouble peeing or any other symptom above. Also go if your symptoms change, get worse or do not feel normal. These symptoms are most often caused by a harmless enlarged prostate, but they still need checking. Men over 40 who know they carry a faulty BRCA2 gene should also see a doctor. You can ask about a PSA blood test even without symptoms, and the doctor will go through the pros and cons with you. In the UK, a doctor who suspects cancer, or sees a high PSA result, may arrange an urgent referral. This does not definitely mean you have cancer.

prostate.screeningText: Finland has no national prostate cancer screening programme. Its national programmes cover only breast, cervical and colorectal cancer. The Cancer Society of Finland says men without symptoms should not routinely have a PSA test. An exception is a good reason, such as a family history. It says the harms of PSA-only screening outweigh the benefits, including false alarms and treating cancers that would never cause harm. In December 2022, the Council of the EU asked member states to evaluate organised screening using PSA plus MRI follow-up. This invites countries to study it; it does not require screening. Finland is running a large trial called ProScreen (120,000 men) to test this. In the UK, screening all men is not recommended. Targeted screening is planned from 2027 in England. It is for men aged 45 to 61 with a BRCA2 gene change and a relevant family history.

testicular.name: Testicular
testicular.blurb: Most common in young men. Rare, and very treatable.
testicular.lede: Testicular cancer is rare. Treatment results are extremely good.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: A lump on a testicle
items.what: A lump you can feel in part of one testicle. It can be as small as a pea, or much larger.

items.title: A swollen or bigger testicle
items.what: One testicle gets bigger or looks swollen compared with how it was before.

items.title: A heavy or hard scrotum
items.what: The skin sac around the testicles feels heavy, firmer or harder than usual.

items.title: Ache or sharp pain
items.what: A dull ache or sudden sharp pain in a testicle or the scrotum. Cancer is often painless, so lack of pain proves nothing.

items.title: Ache in back or lower belly
items.what: A backache or dull ache low in the belly. This can happen if cancer has spread to lymph nodes at the back of the belly.

items.title: Cough or breathing trouble
items.what: A cough, breathlessness, or trouble swallowing, sometimes with a swollen chest. These can mean the cancer has spread to the chest or lungs.

items.title: Swollen or tender breasts
items.what: Some men have tender or swollen breasts, caused by hormones that some testicular cancers make.

items.title: Losing weight without trying
items.what: Weight loss that you cannot explain can be a symptom, usually alongside other symptoms.

symptoms.see: See a doctor if you notice any lump or swelling on a testicle. Also go if a testicle gets bigger, your scrotum feels heavy, firm or hard, or you have an ache or pain. Any change that is not normal for you is worth checking. This includes a lump or change in the soft tube at the back of a testicle. In Finland, every lump or swelling in a testicle is a reason to see a doctor. Most lumps are not cancer, and other causes exist, such as a fluid-filled cyst. Urgent: in young people, sudden pain in the scrotum can be a twisted testicle (torsion). It always needs immediate surgery. Try not to feel embarrassed. Doctors are used to these problems.
symptoms.note: If you suspect testicular cancer, see your doctor.
symptoms.contact: The doctor will feel your testicles, starting with the normal one.

check.title: Feel for changes
text: Cancer Society of Finland: feel both testicles regularly. Cancer Research UK: no need for a set routine. Either way, know what is normal for you.

steps.t: Check during or just after a warm bath or shower, when the scrotum has warmed up and loosened.

steps.h: Hold the scrotum in your palm
steps.t: Cup your scrotum, the skin pouch around the testicles, in the palm of one hand.
steps.look: Compare size, weight and shape. One testicle a little bigger or lower is common.

steps.h: Roll one testicle at a time
steps.t: With your other hand, gently roll one testicle between your thumb and fingers. Then do the other.
steps.look: A healthy testicle is smooth and fairly firm, never hard. Notice any lump, swelling or hard spot.

steps.t: Turn the testicle in your fingers and feel its whole surface for lumps or bumps. Do each side in turn.
steps.look: Bumps or any change in the surface.

steps.t: Feel behind each testicle for the small, soft tube there. This is the epididymis, and it is a normal part of the body.
steps.look: A tube behind the testicle that feels hard, swollen or painful.

steps.t: See a doctor about a lump or swelling, a bigger testicle, a heavy or hard scrotum, pain, or any change that is unusual for you.

normal: A healthy testicle is smooth and firm, though not hard.
One testicle is often a little larger, or hangs a bit lower, than the other.
The surface of a healthy testicle is even, and the testicle slides about freely.
The tube behind each testicle, the epididymis, feels soft and spongy.
Each testicle is roughly the size of a small egg.
Most lumps and changes found are not cancer. Harmless causes include infection, a fluid-filled sac or a swollen vein.
check.found: See a doctor about any lump, swelling, bigger testicle, heavy or hard scrotum, or pain. Most causes are not cancer, but cancer found early is easier to treat. A small painless lump inside the testicle itself is the kind of change doctors take most seriously. Sudden pain in the scrotum can mean a twisted testicle, which needs urgent surgery.

videos.title: Video: How to check your testicles
How can you tell if your testicles are healthy

check.differ: The NHS says to check about once a month from puberty. Cancer Research UK says there is no need for a set routine, because there is little evidence it helps. The Cancer Society of Finland says to feel your testicles regularly. All agree: tell a doctor about any lump, swelling or change.

testicular.screeningText: There is no national screening programme for testicular cancer in the UK, because no reliable test finds it early. Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and colorectal cancer. Checking your own testicles is not the same as screening. The NHS suggests checking about once a month from puberty, ideally during or after a warm bath or shower. Cancer Research UK says there is no need for a set routine. It notes there is little evidence that regular self-checks in a set way help. Both agree it is useful to know what is normal for you and to get any change checked.

lung.name: Lung
lung.blurb: Smoking is the biggest risk. Early signs are easy to miss.
lung.lede: Lung cancer starts in one or both lungs. It is one of the three most common cancers in Finland, and smoking is its biggest risk factor.
lung.screeningText: Finland has no national lung cancer screening programme. Finland's national programmes are only for breast, cervical and colorectal cancer. The Finnish Cancer Registry says CT scans of smokers cut lung cancer deaths by one-fifth. It did not recommend screening, because of many unnecessary follow-up tests. Finland's national lung cancer programme (2026 to 2035) will now look at screening people at higher risk. In England, the NHS offers lung health checks in some areas. They are for people aged 55 to 74 who have ever smoked, and targeted screening is being rolled out. In the UK, the National Screening Committee recommends targeted screening for people at high risk.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: A new or changed cough
items.what: A new cough, a cough that is there most of the time, or an old cough that sounds or feels different.

items.title: Coughing up blood
items.what: Phlegm streaked with blood, or blood spots on a tissue after you cough. This needs urgent medical advice.

items.title: Breathless doing normal things
items.what: You get puffed out doing everyday jobs that you once did with no trouble.

items.title: Chest or shoulder pain
items.what: An ache or pain in your chest or shoulder. Pain in the chest or upper back can be an emergency.

items.title: Chest infections that keep returning
items.what: Chest infections that come back again and again, or one infection that will not clear up.

items.title: Weight loss, low appetite, tiredness
items.what: You lose weight without trying, you do not feel like eating, or you feel tired all the time.

items.title: A hoarse, croaky voice
items.what: Your voice sounds rough or croaky, and it stays that way.

items.title: Swollen face or neck
items.what: Your face or neck looks puffy or swollen. It can come with breathing trouble, especially when you lie on your back.

items.title: Trouble swallowing
items.what: Swallowing becomes difficult.

items.title: Changes in fingertip shape
items.what: Your fingertips look broader than before, or bend downward.

symptoms.see: See a doctor if you have a cough that lasts more than 3 weeks, or any other symptom on this list. Get urgent medical advice if you cough up blood. Get emergency help if you struggle to breathe, or have pain in your chest or upper back. Lung cancer often causes no symptoms early on, and these signs have other common causes. Still, getting checked is important, because finding it early may make it easier to treat.

stomach.name: Stomach
stomach.blurb: Less common than it was. It can stay silent.
stomach.lede: Stomach cancer starts in the stomach, the organ that helps digest food. It has become much less common in Finland, but it can stay silent for a long time.
stomach.screeningText: Finland has no screening programme for stomach cancer. The Finnish Cancer Registry says screening is not considered necessary in countries with few stomach cancers, such as Finland. Finland's national screening programmes are only for breast, cervical and colorectal cancer.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Heartburn or acid reflux
items.what: A burning feeling in your chest after eating, or acid coming back up. Indigestion is common, so watch for changes or no relief.

items.title: Trouble swallowing
items.what: Swallowing hurts or burns, or food seems to get stuck in your throat or chest.

items.title: Feeling full very quickly
items.what: You feel full after eating only a small amount.

items.title: Feeling or being sick
items.what: Nausea or vomiting that keeps coming back. Rarely there is blood in the vomit, bright red or dark brown like coffee grounds.

items.title: Upper tummy pain or lump
items.what: Pain at the top of your tummy, or a lump you can feel there.

items.title: Weight loss and no appetite
items.what: You lose weight without dieting, or you do not feel like eating.

items.title: Dark or almost black poo
items.what: Poo that looks darker than usual, sometimes almost black, from bleeding in the stomach. Iron tablets can also do this.

items.title: Tired and out of breath
items.what: You feel tired with no energy, or short of breath. Slow bleeding can lower red blood cells (anaemia).

items.title: Burping a lot and indigestion
items.what: Lots of burping or an upset stomach that does not settle with your usual remedies.

items.title: Tummy pain spreading to the back
items.what: Steady tummy pain, or pain that spreads from the stomach area through to your back (Finnish Cancer Society).

symptoms.see: See a doctor if you have trouble swallowing, a lump in your tummy, or weight loss you cannot explain by diet or exercise. Also go if stomach symptoms get worse or do not improve after 3 weeks. In Finland the Cancer Society adds more signs. Go if upper-tummy trouble first starts at about 50 to 55 or older. Go too if you vomit again and again, vomit blood, pass black stool, or have new anaemia. Get urgent advice if you are being sick for more than 2 days. Early stomach cancer can feel like other stomach problems, so tell your doctor if your usual symptoms change.

thyroid.name: Thyroid
thyroid.blurb: A lump low in the neck. Most have a good outlook.
thyroid.lede: Thyroid cancer starts in the thyroid, a small gland low in the front of the neck that makes hormones. Most cases have a good outlook.
thyroid.screeningText: Finland has no national screening programme for thyroid cancer. Finland's national screening programmes are only for cervical, breast and colorectal cancer, and the Finnish Cancer Registry's screening page does not mention thyroid. If you find a lump in your neck, see a doctor.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Lump low at front of neck
items.what: A lump low at the front of your neck. It often feels firm, grows slowly and usually does not hurt.

items.title: Neck pain or a pressing feeling
items.what: Pain at the front of your neck, or a sense of weight or pressure on it.

items.title: A hoarse, croaky voice
items.what: Your voice sounds rough or croaky and is not improving.

items.title: Trouble swallowing or breathing
items.what: Swallowing becomes hard, or you feel more short of breath than usual.

items.title: Bumps elsewhere on the neck
items.what: Bumps on other parts of the neck can be swollen lymph glands, if the cancer has spread there.

items.title: Loose poo or flushed face (rare)
items.what: Frequent loose poo, or a red, flushed face. This is rare and is linked to the medullary type.

symptoms.see: See a doctor if you find a lump in your neck, even if it does not hurt. Also go if your voice stays hoarse, swallowing stays difficult, or you have neck pain or a feeling of pressure. See a doctor again if a lump you had checked suddenly grows. Get urgent help if you have trouble breathing or are more short of breath than usual. Most lumps and these symptoms are not cancer, but a check is important because early cancer may be easier to treat.

mouththroat.name: Mouth and throat
mouththroat.blurb: Sores and patches that do not heal.
mouththroat.lede: Mouth cancer can start on the tongue, gums, lips or inside the cheeks. Cancer in the part of the throat just behind the mouth is called oropharyngeal cancer.
mouththroat.screeningText: Finland has no national screening programme for mouth or throat cancer. Finland's national programmes are only for breast, cervical and colorectal cancer. The Finnish guideline says there is little evidence that screening the whole population lowers deaths from mouth cancer. Instead, the lining of the mouth is checked at regular dental visits. A yearly check is advised for some people. These are people over 40 who smoke or drink heavily, or who have risky patches in the mouth.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Mouth sore that will not heal
items.what: A sore or ulcer in the mouth that is still there after 2 to 3 weeks. Early on, it often causes few symptoms.

items.title: Cauliflower-like growth or deep crater
items.what: A bumpy, cauliflower-like growth or deep pit in the mouth lining. It may not hurt, and the area around it often feels harder.

items.title: Red or white patch
items.what: A red patch, a white patch, or a mix of both in your mouth or throat. White patches that rub off are often thrush.

items.title: Lump or hard area in mouth
items.what: A bump or hardened area you can feel inside the mouth or on the lip.

items.title: Crusty patch on the lip
items.what: A crusty, slow-healing spot on the lip, most often the lower lip, that bleeds easily.

items.title: Mouth pain, sometimes reaching the ear
items.what: Ongoing pain in the mouth. Sometimes the first sign is pain on one side that spreads to the ear.

items.title: Loose tooth or ill-fitting denture
items.what: A tooth that wobbles for no clear reason, or dentures that no longer fit.

items.title: Hard to swallow or speak clearly
items.what: Swallowing is hard or painful. Your voice sounds husky or quiet, or you slur some words.

items.title: Lump in the neck
items.what: A lump in the neck that slowly gets bigger. A hot, red, painful lump is more often an infection.

items.title: One-sided sore throat
items.what: A sore throat that lingers, often on one side. One tonsil may look much bigger than the other.

items.title: Bleeding or numbness in the mouth
items.what: Unusual bleeding, or an area of the mouth that feels numb, with no clear reason.

items.title: Losing weight without trying
items.what: Weight loss, sometimes because eating hurts or swallowing is hard.

symptoms.see: See a dentist or doctor about any mouth change that has not gone away in 2 to 3 weeks. Examples are a sore, a red or white patch, or a lump. Others are ongoing pain, trouble swallowing or speaking, a hoarse voice that stays, or a lump in the neck or throat. A dentist can check your mouth too. A neck lump can be a sign of a more advanced cancer. Tests and treatment are then always urgent. In Finland, a yearly mouth check is advised for some people. These are people over 40 who smoke or drink heavily, or who have risky patches in the mouth. Early mouth cancer often causes few symptoms, so regular dental visits matter.

pancreas.name: Pancreas
pancreas.blurb: Often no early signs, so it is usually found late.
pancreas.lede: Pancreatic cancer starts in the pancreas, an organ high up in your tummy that helps with digestion and makes hormones such as insulin. It often causes no early symptoms, so it is usually found late.
pancreas.screeningText: Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and bowel cancer, so pancreatic cancer is not in a national programme. The UK has no national screening for it either, because the cancer is fairly uncommon and the benefits would not outweigh the costs. Some people at high risk may be offered tests, sometimes as part of research. Examples are people with certain inherited gene changes or several close relatives with the cancer.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Yellow skin or eyes
items.what: Skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow. Skin may itch, pee looks darker and poo looks paler than usual.

items.title: Dull ache in the upper tummy
items.what: A dull, gnawing ache high in the tummy. It can reach round to the back and feel worse after meals or when lying flat.

items.title: Weight loss and low appetite
items.what: You lose weight without trying to, and you have little appetite. You may also feel very tired or low on energy.

items.title: Pale, smelly poo
items.what: Poo that is pale, large and smelly, and hard to flush away. This can mean food is not being absorbed well.

items.title: Feeling sick or bloated
items.what: You feel sick or are sick, or feel bloated like you have indigestion. Being sick for more than two days needs urgent checking.

items.title: Signs of new diabetes
items.what: Strong thirst, peeing often and tiredness can be signs of new diabetes, which can come with pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Fever that comes and goes
items.what: A raised temperature that comes and goes, sometimes with chills or shivering.

symptoms.see: Ask for an urgent appointment if you notice yellow skin or yellow whites of the eyes. Do the same if you have been sick for over 2 days or have had diarrhoea for over 7 days. Also see a doctor if you lose a lot of weight without trying. Do so too if symptoms get worse or last more than 2 weeks. Many of these symptoms have other causes, but finding cancer early may make it easier to treat.

liver.name: Liver
liver.blurb: Usually grows in a liver already damaged by disease.
liver.lede: Primary liver cancer starts in the liver, a large organ on the upper right side of your tummy. In Finland it is fairly rare, and it usually grows in a liver already damaged by cirrhosis or another long-term liver disease.
liver.screeningText: Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and bowel cancer, so liver cancer is not in a national programme. The UK has none either, because liver cancer is rare, no suitable test exists and screening would cost a lot. People at high risk may be offered an ultrasound scan every 6 months, sometimes with an AFP blood test. This includes people with cirrhosis or long-term hepatitis B. Advice differs: European guidelines (EASL, ESMO) back 6-monthly ultrasound for people with cirrhosis. The Finnish Terveyskirjasto article says regular scans for all people with cirrhosis have not been shown to change treatment or results.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Yellow skin or eyes
items.what: The skin and whites of the eyes turn yellow, harder to spot on brown or black skin. Skin itches, pee looks darker, poo paler.

items.title: Ache on the upper right side
items.what: An ache high on the right side of the tummy. It can also be felt in the right shoulder.

items.title: A lump on the right side
items.what: A lump you can feel on the right side of your tummy. See a doctor if you notice one.

items.title: A swollen tummy
items.what: The tummy looks and feels swollen. This can bring discomfort, feeling full quickly, breathlessness or swollen feet.

items.title: Weight loss and sickness
items.what: You lose weight without trying, lose your appetite, or feel or are sick. You may feel full after eating very little.

items.title: Tiredness and feeling unwell
items.what: You feel tired, with no energy, or generally unwell, as if you have the flu.

symptoms.see: Ask for an urgent appointment if you notice yellow skin or yellow whites of the eyes. Do the same if you have been sick for over 2 days. See a doctor if you feel a lump in your tummy or lose much weight without meaning to. Also go if your symptoms get worse. If you already have cirrhosis, tell your doctor about any new or worsening symptoms. Early liver cancer often causes no symptoms at all.

kidney.name: Kidney
kidney.blurb: Often found by chance on a scan.
kidney.lede: Kidney cancer starts in the kidneys, the two organs that clean waste and extra fluid out of your blood and turn it into pee. About 1,000 people in Finland are diagnosed each year, and many cases are found by chance on an ultrasound done for another reason.
kidney.screeningText: Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and bowel cancer, so kidney cancer is not in a national programme. The UK has no national screening for it either, and many kidney cancers are found by chance on a scan done for another reason. People from families with rare inherited conditions may be offered a yearly ultrasound or MRI scan of the kidneys. One example is von Hippel-Lindau disease.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Blood in your pee
items.what: Blood in your pee can come and go. Sometimes there is too little to see, but a urine test can find it.

items.title: Pain in the side
items.what: A pain in the side between the ribs and the hip that keeps coming back. It may wrap round to the lower back.

items.title: A lump or swelling
items.what: You may notice a swollen patch or lump on your back, beneath the ribs, or on your neck.

items.title: Weight loss and tiredness
items.what: You lose weight without trying, lose your appetite, and feel very tired or low on energy.

items.title: Fever and heavy sweats
items.what: A fever that lingers, or heavy sweats, including at night.

items.title: Often no symptoms at all
items.what: Most people have no symptoms. The cancer is often spotted by chance on a scan done for something else.

symptoms.see: Ask for an urgent appointment if your pee smells bad, looks cloudy or contains blood. Do the same if peeing hurts, or you need to pee suddenly or more often. Also go urgently for a pain in the back below the ribs that will not go away. The same goes for pain in the genitals, or a lump or swelling in the back, below the ribs or on the neck. These signs can look like a kidney infection, which can become serious without fast treatment. See a doctor too if you lose a noticeable amount of weight, have a fever that will not go away, or feel extremely tired.

bladder.name: Bladder
bladder.blurb: Blood in the pee is the most common sign.
bladder.lede: Bladder cancer starts in the bladder, the organ that stores your pee. Smoking is its main risk factor, and blood in the pee is the most common warning sign.
bladder.screeningText: Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and bowel cancer, so bladder cancer is not in a national programme. The UK has none either, because no test reliably finds bladder cancer early and the benefits would not outweigh the costs. Testing urine for blood is not a useful screening test for the general population, because small amounts of blood can have other causes. The best way to find bladder cancer early is to see a doctor about any bladder symptoms.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Blood in your pee
items.what: Pee that looks pink or red, or rarely dark brown. It is usually painless and may come and go.

items.title: Burning or stinging when peeing
items.what: A sore, burning or stinging feeling when you pee.

items.title: Needing to pee more often
items.what: You need the toilet far more often than usual, or you suddenly need to pee in a hurry.

items.title: Urine infections that keep returning
items.what: Burning or needing to pee often is usually an infection. If it lasts or keeps coming back, doctors need to check further.

items.title: Pain, weight loss and tiredness
items.what: In more advanced cancer, you may have back or lower tummy pain, bone pain, weight loss and tiredness.

symptoms.see: See a doctor if you ever notice blood in your pee. That applies even if it is a small amount, happens only once, or you have no other symptoms. NHS advice is to ask for an urgent appointment. Finnish doctors (Duodecim) say visible blood in the pee always needs tests. Get help at once if peeing becomes difficult, and otherwise on the next working day. Burning or needing to pee often is usually an infection, but if it lasts or keeps coming back, you need more tests.

ovary.name: Ovary
ovary.blurb: Vague early signs, so it is often found late.
ovary.lede: Ovarian cancer starts in the ovaries, two small organs that hold a woman's eggs and make female hormones. Early signs are vague, so it is often found late.
ovary.screeningText: There is no national screening programme for ovarian cancer in the UK, because no test finds it reliably at an early stage. A large UK trial found that ultrasound and the CA125 blood test did not save lives when used as screening. The Cancer Society of Finland also says no method exists to detect the disease early. Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and colorectal cancer. People at high inherited risk (for example BRCA gene changes) can talk to a doctor about their options, which may include preventive surgery.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Swollen or bloated belly
items.what: Your belly looks bigger or feels puffed up and tight. It happens often: roughly 12 or more times in a month.

items.title: Pain low in the belly
items.what: An ache or sore feeling in your lower belly, or in the area between your hip bones.

items.title: Feeling full very quickly
items.what: You eat only a little and feel full, or you simply do not feel like eating.

items.title: Needing to pee more often
items.what: You pee more often than usual, or you suddenly feel you must go straight away.

items.title: Tiredness, bowel or back changes
items.what: Feeling very tired for no reason, loose or hard poo, indigestion, back pain, or weight loss you did not plan.

items.title: Unusual vaginal bleeding
items.what: Bleeding between periods, periods heavier than usual for you, or any bleeding after menopause.

items.title: Pain during sex
items.what: Sex becomes painful. This can happen when a growing tumour presses on nearby organs.

items.title: Short of breath or cough
items.what: Sometimes the first sign is breathlessness, a cough or chest pain. This can mean the cancer has reached the lung lining.

symptoms.see: See a doctor if you have any of these symptoms, especially if they are new for you, keep coming back, or get worse. They are common and often have other causes, but checking early matters. Tell the doctor if ovarian or breast cancer runs in your family. In the UK, a doctor who suspects cancer may arrange an urgent referral, usually within 2 weeks. This does not mean you definitely have cancer. Unusual vaginal bleeding, including bleeding after menopause, is one of the signs to get checked.

womb.name: Womb
womb.blurb: Bleeding is the main sign. Often found early.
womb.lede: Womb cancer, also called endometrial cancer, usually starts in the lining of the womb. It is most common after menopause and is often found early because it causes bleeding.
womb.screeningText: There is no national screening programme for womb cancer in the UK, because no test can pick it up early. A vaginal ultrasound or womb biopsy has not been shown to work in women without symptoms. Finland's national screening programmes cover only breast, cervical and colorectal cancer, and the cervical smear does not find womb cancer. For women with Lynch syndrome, UK doctors may offer yearly checks from age 35. Finnish guidance also suggests yearly follow-up from age 35, with a sample of the womb lining.

symptoms.title: Watch for

items.title: Bleeding after menopause
items.what: Spotting or bleeding from the vagina once your periods have stopped for good. This is the most typical sign.

items.title: Periods much heavier than usual
items.what: Your periods become clearly heavier than is normal for you. In women who still have periods, this can be the first sign.

items.title: Bleeding between periods
items.what: Spotting or bleeding at times when you do not expect a period.

items.title: A change in vaginal discharge
items.what: Discharge that looks different from your usual. It may be pink.

items.title: Lump or swelling in the belly
items.what: A lump or swelling in your tummy or between your hip bones. Some people also feel bloated.

items.title: Pelvic or lower back pain
items.what: An ache in your lower back, or in the area between your hip bones.

items.title: Pain during sex
items.what: Sex becomes painful, which is new for you.

items.title: Changes in pee or poo habits
items.what: You go to the toilet more often, or less often, than usual.

symptoms.see: See a doctor as soon as you notice any of these symptoms. Do not wait, and try not to feel embarrassed. Doctors and nurses are used to talking about them. Bleeding after menopause needs checking. If you take tamoxifen, tell your doctor about any unexpected bleeding. Tell the doctor if you or your family have had cancer or Lynch syndrome. In the UK, a doctor who suspects cancer may arrange an urgent referral. This does not definitely mean you have cancer.

FAQ.q: When do I get a mammogram letter?
FAQ.a: Every woman aged 50 to 69 is invited by personal letter, about every 2 years. The letter gives a time and a place.

Contact your health centre about any of these: a lump in the breast or armpit, a change in the shape of the breast, dimpling of the skin, a rash or broken skin on the areola, a nipple that turns inwards or discharge from the nipple, or redness or swelling of the breast.

FAQ.q: Can I take the sample at home?
FAQ.a: In some counties you can take the cervical screening sample at home, as part of a study run by Fimlab in 2026. You need a screening invitation first.
In 2026 people aged 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 70 and 72 are invited, in the counties on Fimlab’s 2026 list. All ages 56 to 74 will be invited by 2031.
Yes. The screening tests organised by wellbeing services counties are free of charge and voluntary.

FAQ.q: Do I have to take part?
FAQ.a: No. Taking part is voluntary. If you do not intend to take part, tell the screening unit using the instructions in your invitation.
If you cannot make the appointment, you can change it. If you do not intend to take part, tell the screening unit using the instructions in your invitation.
You are invited to all screening tests that concern you by letter. The invitation to breast and cervical screening states the time and place. The bowel cancer test kit arrives with the invitation.

FAQ.q: What should I look out for?
FAQ.a: Look out for a lump in the testicle, one testicle getting bigger, a change in how firm a testicle feels, or pain. If you suspect testicular cancer, see your doctor.

FAQ.q: How can I lower my cancer risk?
FAQ.a: The European Code Against Cancer, 5th edition, lists 14 recommendations for you: do not use tobacco, keep smoke away from you, avoid excess weight, be active, eat a healthy diet, avoid alcohol, breastfeed, protect yourself from the sun, know the cancer risks at work, check for radon at home, cut your exposure to air pollution, get vaccinated and tested for cancer-causing infections, be careful with hormone therapy for menopause, and join organised cancer screening.

Cancer happens when cells in your body keep growing without proper control. A group of abnormal cells can form a tumour. Cancer is not one disease. There are more than 200 types, and their causes and behaviour differ a lot.

The stage of a cancer tells how far it has grown and spread. Doctors often use the TNM system, which looks at the size of the main tumour, spread to nearby lymph nodes and spread to other parts of the body. The result is a stage from 0 to IV.
