breast.intro: Breast screening uses a quick X-ray called a mammogram to look for breast cancer before you can feel or see anything. Finding it early gives more treatment choices, and in Finland screening has lowered deaths from breast cancer.

steps.t: If you are a woman aged 50 to 69, a personal letter comes to your home about every two years. It gives the time and place of your mammogram, usually a couple of weeks ahead. It is free, and taking part is voluntary.
steps.tip: The place may be a health and social services centre or a medical centre.

steps.h: Change the time, or say no
steps.t: The letter explains how to book or change the time. It is your choice to go or not. If you skip, your next letter still comes two years later. There are fair reasons both to go and to decline.
steps.tip: You can change the time by phone or online.

steps.t: Have a movement difficulty or a question? Contact the imaging unit before your visit. Imaging usually works in a wheelchair or sitting on a chair. Breasts can be extra sore before a period, so you can ask for a time after it.
steps.tip: Tell the nurse about any fears or worries so they can help.

steps.t: The whole visit takes about five minutes, with a few minutes for the pictures. An X-ray nurse, called a radiographer, guides you. You answer a few health questions, such as about earlier mammograms. You undress, then you are led to the machine.
steps.tip: Tunne rintasi has a video of the visit, also in English.

steps.t: The radiographer places one breast between two plates and presses it flat for about 10 seconds. Pictures are taken from above and from the side, usually standing. Then the other breast follows. People feel it differently: some find it painful, others hardly notice.
steps.tip: UK guide (NHS): you can ask to stop at any time.

steps.t: When the pictures are done, you get dressed and go home. Two radiologists, doctors who read X-rays, study the pictures on their own. If at least one sees something unusual, they look together. Your result is then sent to you.

Your result is sent to you within about a month, usually by letter. In Helsinki you get a text message if you have agreed to it. About 97 in 100 women have a normal result. Then your next invitation comes in two years.

Fewer than 3 in 100 women are called back for more tests, such as extra pictures, an ultrasound or a needle sample. Most do not have breast cancer: about 1 in 5 does. If doubt remains, you get a hospital referral.
steps.tip: Waiting for follow-up tests and results can feel heavy. That is a known downside of screening.

steps.t: Screening does not find every cancer. About a quarter of breast cancers in screened women are found between screenings. See a doctor if you notice a new lump, skin pitting, nipple discharge or lasting pain, even after a normal result.
steps.tip: Do not wait for your next letter. Most lumps are not cancer, but get them checked.

benefits: In Finland, breast cancer deaths were 22% lower among women invited to screening (1992 to 2003), and 28% lower among women who actually went.
Screening prevents about 50 breast cancer deaths in Finland every year.
In women aged 50 to 69, about two thirds of the breast cancers that are found come from screening.
Cancers found early give more chance of breast-sparing surgery and lighter treatment. Over 90% of breast cancers found early can be cured.
downsides: False alarms: about 1 in 5 women who go regularly are called for extra tests at least once that turn out not to be needed. Waiting can be stressful.
Overdiagnosis: screening can find small cancers that would never have caused harm, at most 1 in 10 of those found. All are treated, because nobody can tell which are harmless.
The squeeze can be uncomfortable or painful. The X-ray dose is very small (one Finnish county calls it negligible). Screening also does not find every cancer.
breast.unsure: Going is your choice, it is free, and there are fair reasons both to go and to decline. You can change the time if it does not suit you, or tell the screening unit you do not want to take part, and you will still get a new letter in two years. If you feel nervous, tell the nurse before you start: they can take your worries into account.

cervical.intro: Cervical screening checks cells from the cervix, the neck of the womb, for changes that could turn into cancer years later. In Finland, finding and treating these changes early has cut cervical cancer cases by about 80%.

steps.t: Women aged 30 to 65 are invited every five years. Some counties also invite 25-year-olds. Your personal invitation may come as a Suomi.fi or OmaPosti message, or as a paper letter. It is free and voluntary.
steps.tip: In Fimlab's area, no invitation by the end of September? Contact Fimlab customer service.

steps.t: Many counties, such as HUS in Uusimaa, pre-book a time for you. You can change or cancel it online or by phone, using the key and PIN in your letter. Other counties ask you to book your own time. Taking part is your choice.
steps.tip: In Fimlab's area, book online any time or call 010 808 515 on weekdays 7 to 16.

steps.h: A home kit, if you prefer
steps.t: In Central Finland, Kanta-Häme, Ostrobothnia, Pirkanmaa and Päijät-Häme, you can join a 2026 study and use a home kit instead of a clinic visit. You take a sample yourself from the vagina with a thin stick and post it within 24 hours.
steps.tip: You need your invitation to order the kit. A positive result means a clinic sample next.

steps.t: Fill in the health form from your invitation. You cannot give the sample during your period. Skip vaginal suppositories the day before and the day of the test. A normal pregnancy up to week 35 and a past hysterectomy do not stop you.
steps.tip: Lost the form? You can answer its questions at the visit.

steps.t: A nurse trained in screening samples takes your sample. First you hand in your health form and show an ID, such as your Kela card. The whole visit takes about 10 minutes. The sampling itself only takes a couple of minutes.
steps.tip: Mobility difficulty, or sampling went badly before? Tell customer service before your visit.

steps.t: The nurse places a speculum, a small tool shaped like a duck's beak, in the vagina so the cervix can be seen. A soft brush collects cells. Expect a stretch and a small pinch. Light spotting may follow for a couple of days.
steps.tip: UK guide (NHS): you can ask to stop at any time, and bring someone for support.

steps.t: Your sample is tested for high-risk HPV if you are 30 or older. You get the result within about two months, mostly online or by post. More than 9 in 10 results are normal. Then your next invitation comes in about five years.
steps.tip: No result after three months? Contact the screening laboratory's customer service.

steps.t: About 5 in 100 women are asked to repeat the test in 1 to 2 years. About 1 in 100 is invited for a colposcopy: a close look at the cervix, with tissue samples. Almost always the cause is mild changes that are not cancer.
steps.tip: If a biopsy shows a precancer, a procedure removes the changed area.

steps.t: Early cervical cancer often has no symptoms, which is why screening matters. See a doctor if you have irregular bleeding, unusual discharge that is bloody, brown or smelly, or bleeding after sex. Do not wait for your next invitation.
steps.tip: HPV vaccinated? You should still take part in screening, says HUS.

benefits: Screening has cut new cervical cancer cases in Finland by 80%.
It is estimated to avoid more than 250 cancer deaths in Finland each year.
Screening finds over 600 cancer precursors and early cancers in Finland every year, and these can all be cured.
Most cervical cancers are found in women who did not take part in screening.
downsides: About 1 in 3 women who go regularly has an abnormal finding at least once that needs follow-up. Most are mild, but waiting can be stressful.
The sample can feel like a stretch and a small pinch, and light spotting may last a couple of days.
A positive HPV test can feel scary, but an HPV infection usually clears up by itself within a couple of years.
cervical.unsure: Many women feel nervous about this test, and the visit is short: about 10 minutes, with the sampling taking a couple. You can tell the nurse how you feel, and UK guidance says you can ask to stop at any time. You can also change the time, decline, or in five counties in 2026 ask for a home kit instead: it is your choice, and it is free.

bowel.intro: Bowel cancer often has no signs in its early stages. This stool test, done at home, looks for tiny amounts of blood you cannot see, which can be an early warning.

steps.t: In 2026, people turning 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 70 and 72 are invited. Your personal letter comes every two years, with a sample kit and instructions inside. Screening will grow to all ages 56 to 74 by 2031. It is free and voluntary.
steps.tip: Fimlab sends by birth month: spring births in spring, summer births in summer, later ones by end of November.

steps.t: You do not need to change what you eat. Read the instructions and watch the video. Fill in the information form that came with your letter, mostly online. Choose a day that suits you.
steps.tip: Tube frozen in winter? Let it thaw at room temperature before taking the sample.

steps.h: Taking the sample, step by step
steps.t: Use a clean surface, like a paper plate, never the toilet bowl. Open the green cap, without touching the liquid inside, and brush the stick 2 to 3 times over the stool until its tip is covered. Click the cap shut and shake the tube.
steps.tip: Hard stool? Dampen it with a little water. Loose stool? Dry the stick with toilet paper first.

steps.t: Write the date on the label and stick it along the tube. Put the tube in its pouch, and the pouch in the return envelope with the paper form if you used one. Post it within 24 hours of taking the sample. Postage is prepaid.
steps.tip: Check your letter. In the HUS area, you drop it in a lab box, no booking.

steps.t: The lab looks for hidden blood in your sample. You get the result about one month after posting it, mainly as a Suomi.fi or OmaPosti message, or as a paper letter. It also shows in MyKanta from 9 March 2026.
steps.tip: Questions about your result? Ask your local health centre or screening contact person.

steps.t: More than 9 in 10 results are normal. That means no blood was found and you need no more tests. Your next invitation comes in two years, because the test only shows how you are now.
steps.tip: A normal test is not a lifetime guarantee. See a doctor about bowel symptoms.

steps.t: About 4 in 100 people have blood found in their sample. This usually does not mean cancer, but the cause must be found. Your letter tells you how to reach your local screening nurse, who sets up the next test, usually a colonoscopy.
steps.tip: Blood can have harmless causes, such as haemorrhoids (piles).

steps.t: Beforehand, you empty your bowel as instructed so the doctor can see clearly. A thin bendable tube with a camera goes in through the bottom, with sedation or anaesthesia. It takes 20 minutes to 1 hour. The doctor can take samples and remove small growths.
steps.tip: Afterwards you may feel bloated. No driving or cycling until the next day.

steps.t: The test checks only for hidden blood. If you have symptoms or worries, do not wait for your next invitation: contact your doctor. Symptoms can include blood or mucus in your stool, belly pain, changes in how your bowel works or trouble passing stool.
steps.tip: Symptoms can build slowly and are easy to miss.

benefits: Current knowledge: screening can prevent about 1 in 6 bowel cancer deaths (Fimlab). Suomi.fi gives a range of 10% to 40% fewer deaths.
It can find growths before they turn into cancer, and removing them can stop cancer from forming.
Cancers found early are usually easier to treat: less invasive surgery, no stoma and no chemotherapy.
It is easy and does not hurt: one sample at home, no food rules, free. In 2024, 73.5% of invited people took part.
downsides: False alarms: about 4 in 100 tests show blood. The cause is often harmless, such as piles, but a colonoscopy is usually needed to find out.
A colonoscopy is an invasive test. It needs bowel emptying first, and has a small risk of infection, bleeding or a tear in the bowel wall.
A normal result only shows how you are now. The test is repeated every two years, and symptoms in between still need a doctor.
bowel.unsure: This test is free, done at home and does not hurt, but it is still your choice. You can take the sample at any time that suits you, or decide not to take part: if you do not, you get two reminders, and the next invitation comes two years later. If you already have regular colonoscopies, you do not need this test.

content.STATS_NOTE: These are model estimates for 2024 from national cancer registry data. "1 in 10" means about 10 out of every 100 people in that group are diagnosed before they turn 75, if they live that long. It is an average. Your own chance depends on your age, family history, lifestyle and more, and it does not mean you will or will not get cancer.

hpv.name: HPV vaccine
hpv.protects: HPV causes cervical cancer and some other cancers.

hbv.name: Hepatitis B vaccine
hbv.protects: Long-term hepatitis B can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer. The vaccine prevents the infection.
hbv.finland: In Finland the hepatitis B vaccine is free for defined risk groups. Anyone else can get it at their own expense, for example at a health centre or a private clinic.

TRIAGE.watchIntro: I only suggest keeping watch when all of these are true: it is a cough, an ache or pain, or a general feeling; it started in the past week; it is mild and getting better; and nothing on my warning list came up. For everything else I suggest telling a doctor, even if it is getting better.

rules.h: Blood, a new lump, or a change in an organ
rules.t: Blood in poo, pee, phlegm or from the vagina, a new lump, and changes in a breast, testicle, mole, bowel or bladder habit, swallowing or weight are the signs cancer guidelines ask doctors to take seriously. The cause is usually harmless, but a doctor should decide. I do not suggest waiting on these.

The NHS says most diarrhoea stops within 5 to 7 days and needs a doctor if it lasts more than 7 days or comes with blood. Cancer guidelines add that a lasting change in bowel habit is a referral sign. This app is about spotting cancer early, so I am more careful than a general stomach-bug page: I suggest mentioning even a short spell that is already getting better. A short call or message to a nurse is enough.

rules.h: A cough or a hoarse voice
rules.t: A cough that lasts 3 weeks or more, or comes with blood, breathlessness, chest pain or weight loss, should be checked. A fresh cough that is easing can be watched for a short while.
Pain that is strong, wakes you at night, lasts more than a week, or is getting worse is worth a doctor. A mild ache that started recently and is easing can be watched.
Anything that is getting worse, or is 7 out of 10 or stronger, is worth contacting a doctor about soon.

breast.name: Breast check
breast.rec: Regularly, whatever your age. There is no fixed schedule: what matters is knowing what is normal for you.
breast.note: Know what is normal for you.

testicular.name: Testicle check
testicular.rec: Feel both testicles regularly. The Cancer Society of Finland gives no fixed interval.
testicular.note: Know what is normal for you.

skin.name: Skin and mole check
skin.short: a couple of times a year
skin.freq: A couple of times a year
skin.rec: Check your skin at home a couple of times a year, and get to know your moles.

SCANS.name: Mammogram
SCANS.where: A health centre or medical centre, named in your invitation letter
SCANS.what: An X-ray of each breast, taken by a radiographer. Each breast is pressed flat for about 10 seconds. Two radiologists read the pictures.
SCANS.note: A national group proposed in March 2025 to widen the ages to 46–74. Check the current ages.

SCANS.name: Cervical screening sample
SCANS.type: Clinical examination (sample taken by a nurse)
SCANS.who: Women aged 30 to 65, in some counties from 25
SCANS.where: A health centre or screening clinic named in your invitation. Home sampling is being studied in some counties in 2026
SCANS.what: A nurse trained in screening takes a small sample of cells from the cervix with a soft brush. It is tested for high-risk HPV.

SCANS.name: Bowel screening test (FIT)
SCANS.who: Ages 56 to 74, phased in by 2031. In 2026: ages 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 70 and 72
SCANS.time: At home, when you choose. Post it within 24 hours
SCANS.where: At home. The kit comes with your invitation letter and you post the sample to the lab
SCANS.what: A stool sample that you take at home. The lab looks for blood you cannot see. More than 9 in 10 results are normal.
SCANS.note: Bowel screening is rolling out by age and county.

SCANS.name: Colonoscopy
SCANS.type: Examination with a camera, at a hospital or clinic
SCANS.who: Only if a doctor refers you, for example after a bowel screening test finds blood
SCANS.freq: No routine schedule. Your doctor decides
SCANS.time: 20 minutes to 1 hour, plus preparing the day before
SCANS.where: A hospital or clinic. Your local screening nurse or doctor arranges it
SCANS.what: A thin, bendable tube with a camera goes in through the bottom, with sedation, so the doctor can see the bowel. Samples can be taken and small growths removed.
SCANS.note: You empty your bowel beforehand as instructed so the doctor can see clearly.

SCANS.name: Low-dose CT lung scan
SCANS.who: Not offered as screening in Finland. Some countries scan older people who have smoked
SCANS.freq: Not a routine test in Finland
SCANS.what: The Finnish Cancer Registry says CT scans of smokers cut lung cancer deaths by one-fifth, but it did not recommend screening because of many unnecessary follow-up tests.
SCANS.note: Finland’s national lung cancer programme (2026 to 2035) will look at screening people at higher risk. In England, lung health checks are offered in some areas to people aged 55 to 74 who have ever smoked.

SCANS.name: PSA blood test
SCANS.who: Men with symptoms or a good reason such as family history. Not for routine testing of men without symptoms
SCANS.freq: Not a routine test. Talk to your doctor
SCANS.what: The Cancer Society of Finland says the harms of PSA-only screening, such as false alarms and treating cancers that would never cause harm, outweigh the benefits.
SCANS.note: The Council of the EU asked countries in 2022 to evaluate organised screening with PSA plus MRI. Finland is running a large trial called ProScreen.

SCANS.name: Skin check by a specialist
SCANS.who: People at higher risk of skin cancer. There is no national melanoma screening
SCANS.what: A doctor looks at your skin and moles. The best way to find melanoma early is to know the signs and see a doctor if you notice any.

breast.pose: Anywhere private: in bed, in the shower, or at a mirror.
breast.move: Nothing to do yet. Pick a time when your breasts are soft, just after a period.

breast.pose: Standing at a mirror, arms relaxed by your sides.
breast.move: Look at both breasts. Slowly turn to each side and look again.
Raise both arms above your head, hold, then lower them. Look from the front and from each side.

breast.pose: Standing at the mirror with your hands on your hips.
breast.move: Press your hands firmly into your hips so your chest muscles tighten. Keep your shoulders straight.
Look closely at each nipple for fluid, crusting, or a change in shape.

breast.pose: Lying on your back, the arm on the side you are checking behind your head. A pillow under that shoulder helps.
breast.move: Rest your other hand flat on the breast you are checking.

breast.pose: Lying on your back, arm behind your head.
breast.move: Press with three flat finger pads and move in small circles, about the size of a coin.
At each spot press three times: lightly, then with medium pressure, then firmly until you feel the ribs.
Move up and down in rows, like mowing a lawn, from your collarbone to your bra line and from your armpit to your breastbone.

breast.pose: Standing in the shower, the arm on the side you are checking raised.
breast.move: Glide soapy fingers over the breast in small circles. Repeat with your arm by your side, then stretched out.

breast.pose: Standing or lying, the arm on the side you are checking raised.
breast.move: Feel all around the nipple, then sweep flat fingers up and down your armpit.

breast.pose: At home, when you are ready.
breast.move: Book an appointment at your health centre.

testicular.pose: Standing or sitting in a warm bath or shower.
testicular.move: Let the warm water relax the skin for a few minutes.

testicular.pose: Standing, with your scrotum resting in the palm of one hand.
testicular.move: Gently lift and hold it. Compare the size and weight of the two sides.

testicular.pose: Standing, one testicle held between your thumb and two fingers.
testicular.move: Roll it slowly between your thumb and fingers, like a small egg.
Slide your fingertips over the whole surface, front and back, and feel for lumps or bumps.
Slide a finger up and down behind the testicle, over the soft tube. Then do the other side.

testicular.pose: At home, when you are ready.
testicular.move: Book an appointment at your health centre.

skin.pose: Standing in a bright room with a full-length mirror and a hand mirror.
skin.move: Look at your skin from head to toe, front and back.
Part your hair with a comb to see your scalp. Check your ears, face and lips.

skin.pose: Standing or sitting, hands in front of you.
skin.move: Turn your hands over, spread your fingers, and look at every nail.

skin.pose: Standing at the mirror, one arm raised.
skin.move: Look at your neck and chest. Lift your breasts to see the skin underneath.
Bend an elbow to see the upper arm, and raise your arm to see the armpit.

skin.pose: Standing with your back to the big mirror.
skin.move: Hold the hand mirror so you can see your neck and back in the big mirror. Turn slowly.

skin.pose: Sitting on a chair or the edge of the bed.
skin.move: Check your bottom and the backs of your legs. Lift each foot to see the sole and the gaps between toes.

skin.pose: At the mirror, or with a photo.
skin.move: Compare each mole against the five ABCDE signs.

skin.pose: Looking at all your moles together.
skin.move: Find the one mole that looks different from the rest.

skin.pose: Standing, with a ruler or tape beside the spot.
skin.move: Take a photo of anything unusual, with the ruler next to it.

skin.pose: At home, when you are ready.
skin.move: Book an appointment at your health centre.
